speechtext:
['Mr. Chairman, I hesitated to say anything earlier in this debate, although the question of external affairs is one in which I am deeply interested. There is a great deal to be said in regard to the matter that was referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and by the hon. member for North Battleford. It is amazing that any hon. member in this house could speak so lightly at this time on that question, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw did in the question he asked. It shows a callousness of mind and an emotional immaturity that is hardly understandable in an hon. member of this house.
As the hour is late I shall emphasize only two points. First, I believe that our future depends on working out a foreign policy along with the other nations of the world.
The Prime Minister this morning stated that the time was approaching when we must begin to shape the outline of the new world that is to follow after the war. It is to be regretted that he did not give us more information in regard to what the government's policies are. I believe the time has

Supply-External Affairs
come when we must begin to formulate policies, and in that regard I would say our approach this time must be different from what it was in the period between the last war and the beginning of the present war.
If we are to have a successful international policy-and when I say "we", I mean Canada in cooperation with the other nations of the world'-we must have a positive policy. The trouble with our policy in the period between the first world war and the second world war was that it was not a positive policy for peace; it was a negative policy to avoid war. I well remember the stock answer that we were given in the house when we asked questions about the government's attitude toward such matters as the Spanish affair, or about the shipment of war material to Japan. We were always told by the Prime Minister that his great concern was to avoid war, not to do anything that would give cause for offence. That was the sort of attitude that led to the present war.
I am firmly convinced that the democratic nations of Europe, Great Britain and France particularly, although they are largely responsible for the war, did not wish war, did not want war. did not consciously prepare for it. They were set on maintaining things as they were, of maintaining their privileges, their place in the world. They allowed the aggressors to prosper in order that the armed forces of Germany would crush a workers' revolution, of which they were afraid. Let me repeat that the essential thing in a new foreign policy to prevent war is that in the first place it will be a positive policy.
I am very happy to-night to find myself in accord with nearly all that was said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I think he made a most excellent speech and said many things that needed to be said. I agree with the statement that we must put our trust in a system of collective security when this war is over. I believe also that we must begin building that collective security system now. I see no hope for security for Canada in any combination outside a collective security system that will give security not only to Canada but to every nation in the world.
I was surprised this morning to hear the hon. member for Vancouver South say that the British commonwealth of nations and the United States should form an alliance, and that they should tell the world that they are forming an alliance. I admit the sincerity of the hon. member's approach to the question; but to my mind nothing could be more dangerous at this time than for two of the powerful partners in the united nations to say that they intend to form a close alliance. If the United States and the British commonwealth of nations, two of the large units in the united nations, will form an alliance, what is to prevent Russia and China from forming an alliance? We would have again the same old power blocks, one against the other.
I may not know a great deal about international affairs, but I submit that that is not the way in which world peace can be maintained. We have before us a choice of one of two things. We have a choice of being a partner in a system of collective security, where each nation in that collective system will have protection against aggression from any quarter, or we can go along forming alliances and building up balances of power, which policy will ultimately lead to a war such as that in which we are now engaged. Any system of security will also have to be one based on the equality of the nations.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said this evening that we of the British empire, or the British commonwealth of nations, whichever you like, were a very fine people, indeed, but that unfortunately the rest of the world did not have the exalted opinion of our virtues that we have ourselves. I was recently talking to a gentleman who holds a high position in this country. Some three years ago he had taken advantage of an opportunity of flying from the United Kingdom to Australia by the usual route-Lisbon, along the Mediterranean, crossing to Egypt and Persia and India, and then along the South Sea islands to Australia. He told me that in all the places visited on that trip he did not meet any native peoples who were friendly to the British empire. He said that where they were not neutral as to which of the warring nations they would have rule them, they were definitely hostile. His statement was that their attitude was largely owing to the superior attitude adopted by the people Britain had sent to those countries as governors.
AVhat is said by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques) may be quite true, namely, that by and large the British government has given government as good as or better than any other country. The fact remains, however, that the British government was ruling larger sections of the world than any other country, and governments are usually unpopular. The government you have not is usually better than the one you have.
The War-Sicily', 'The British empire has a great deal for which it is responsible, because it has had tremendous opportunities.
The hour is late, and I do not wish to say anything further, except that I want again to emphasize that if we are to reap the fruits of the sacrifices of this war; if we are to get some return in peace and prosperity for the young lives that are being sacrificed in this war, we shall get it only through a system of collective security, in which each nation- Canada included-will become a guarantor for the peace and safety of all nations.
Item stands.
Progress reported.']

Yesterday on the orders of the day the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) inquired about deliveries of coal from dealers to consumers in Toronto. The matter of deliveries of coal from dealers to consumers in Toronto and elsewhere in Canada falls within the jurisdiction of the wartime prices and trade board, through the services administrator and the coal administrator. The recommendations of the Canadian Retail Coal Dealers' Association, recently convened in Toronto, have been submitted to the coal controller of the Department of Munitions and Supply. These proposals have received serious consideration, and a course of action is being planned. The plans have been further reviewed in conjunction with the wartime prices and trade board and a representative group of Ontario and Quebec dealers, and are now receiving final consideration. Action wil be taken on these proposals in the near future.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and other members of the house have asked me if I would make, when it came to a discussion of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, a somewhat fuller statement on the war situation than it was possible to make earlier in the session. Hon. members also at different times have requested that in dealing with the estimates of external affairs I should take up particular subjects which they have specified. I have thought that it would facilitate the discussions in committee were I to anticipate as far as possible the information with which hon. members would wish to be supplied. I shall therefore first of all very briefly review significant and recent developments in the war situation, and follow that by statements with reference to the united nations organization and planning, the agencies for the direction of the war effort, the planning of the settlement which may follow the ending of
hostilities, the refugee situation, and Canada's diplomatic representation; I shall also later in the discussions give to the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) the information which he asked I should let him have with respect to the Alaska highway and the pipeline from the Fort William oil fields to the refinery at White Horse.
In the earlier part of the session, and especially in the statement which I made on February 1, I reviewed in some detail the known proceedings of the Casablanca conference between Mr. Churchill, President Roosevelt, and various officers of the armed forces of both nations.
I called attention also to various developments in the means and usages of consultation and conference among the governments of the united nations. I suggested that some of the gaps, in these means of consultation, would have to be filled in as the further planning of offensive warfare progressed. What I am about to say relates to developments of the last few months and especially to the mounting successes in the offensive warfare of the united nations.
During most of the months between May of 1940 and August of 1942, the story of the war was mainly one of aggression succeeding aggression in many parts of the world. In no aspect of the general picture of the war in 1942 was there any more significant departure than the extent to which the united nations were able to take the offensive on a large and sustained scale against the axis.
In many areas throughout the summer of 1942, battle forces were so evenly matched that in any particular theatre, even a slight alteration of forces, even a slight accession of concentrated strength, might have tilted the balance towards victory or defeat. As late as mid-October, I felt it was necessary to say that there was no sign that the tide of war had definitely turned. We know now to what extent good use was made of those months from June to October in supplying reinforcements and equipment to a few areas in which a later offensive against the axis might be launched. We know now how careful and precise was the planning which, once the initiative had been taken, made it possible for the offensive to be sustained.
That offensive marked the first turning of the tide in the great battle around the world. The main offensive phase began in the southwest Pacific with the American landings in the Solomons in August, 1942. It was continued, nearer the European fortress, in the offensive launched by the British Eighth
Supply-External

Affairs-War Situation
Army, westward from: El Alamein, late in October. It received its greatest impetus from the allied landings, in Morocco and Algeria, early in November.
On May 10, in introducing a resolution of congratulation on the victory of the allied forces, I reviewed the campaign in North Africa in some detail. I shall not say more of it to-day. The results are well known. They mark the triumphal close of an allimportant chapter in the war.
Elsewhere, campaigns which were holding actions on a vast scale have been turned against the original aggressors with increasing force. In Russia, what looked' for a long time like a last-ditch defensive stand was turned into an offensive of such proportions that the entire German Sixth Army was annihilated at Stalingrad. Losses of men and materials on this front have been heavier than in any other theatre of operations. Before the end of 1942, at various points: at the eastern edge of the Black Sea, in the Don valley, on the central front, and in the northwest _ region fronting on the Baltic, steady gains had been made by Russian forces.
On January 18 of this year, while talks between Mr. Churchill and President Roosevelt were continuing at Casablanca, the siege of Leningrad was lifted. Until the present week, for many weeks past, the front in Russia has been relatively quiet. During the present week, a new German offensive has been launched along nearly 200 miles of the central front. It, along with the recent intensified bombings of strategic areas over Europe, marks a place of new beginning in the war in Europe.
In the Pacific area, Japan's hold remains widespread. There have been some local gains by China in freeing her soil, though the Chinese effort is sharply limited by supplies available, and even more by the length and the difficulties of the supply routes into China. The organization of free China, and the maintenance of industries, education, social ser-vices-many of which migrated for hundreds of miles-has been one of the most resourceful answers to aggression in the history of the world.
In the great area of sea and islands in the south west Pacific, the power of Japan has been held at bay, and losses have been inflicted upon her shipping greater than her present capacity to replace it. United States forces have recently driven the Japanese out of some of their strongholds in the Solomon islands. By a determined initiative, they have

denied to Japan other bases and harbours which might be used to attack Australia or to prey upon the sea routes from the United States to Australia and the Indian ocean. Forces of Australia and New Zealand have joined in fighting the Japanese in New Guinea and other islands to the north of Australia.
One other area, much closer to our own shores, deserves more than passing mention. As a part of Japan's attempt to control the Pacific, her naval and air forces reached out, during 1942, into the Aleutian islands. The Japanese made determined efforts to build and fortify bases for submarines, seaplanes, and other aircraft at Attu and Kiska. During the latter part of May, following initial landings on May 11, Japanese forces were driven out of Attu island, which is now under American control. Kiska remains a potential centre of attack upon our shores, and upon other parts of this continent. To combat this menace, squadrons of the Royal Canadian Air Force, based in Alaska, have been operating continuously in conjunction with United States forces.
From all of the developments of the past eight months, from what is known of decisions taken at Casablanca and during Mr. Churchill's visit to Washington in May, and from the combined planning which continues from day to day, the picture of the war in 1943 emerges more clearly. Germany and Italy have been driven out of Africa. In addition to the loss of all her African territories, Italy has had to relinquish Pantelleria, and other islands in the central Mediterranean. The aerial and commando assaults against Italy and Sicily, against Sardinia and Crete, are parts of a single strategy which the immediate future may be expected rapidly to unfold.
The war in 1943 must be thought of as a vital part of the war of liberation of the oppressed countries of Europe, of which the liberation of the French empire in Africa was both an essential and a memorable prelude.
I shall now come to speak of the united nations organization and planning.
The supreme direction of the war, the coordination of the war effort of the united nations, and the planning of certain aspects of the post-war period and the peace, are all matters which are engaging the attention of appropriate boards or committees representing the united nations.
The united nations have no formal organization. In the prosecution of the 'war they

Supply-External Affairs-War Situation
act together by constant consultation through the usual channels between governments. These channels are supplemented by a series of international advisory bodies which have been set up to facilitate rapid agreement and speedy execution of joint plans. Canada now has very extensive machinery for consultation with the other united nations. Through the Canadian high commissioners in all the countries of the British commonwealth, through the Canadian ministers in the United States, the Soviet Union, China, and diplomatic relations with other allied governments, and through the high commissioners and ministers of the united nations represented in Ottawa, we have the equipment for constant day to day consultation regarding the conduct of the war and the framing of the peace. In addition we have the continually improving methods of consultation and cooperation by direct exchange of cables between governments.
These channels of communication have been supplemented, especially in London and in Washington, by enlarging staffs and by establishing missions representing particular Canadian departments and services, such as the joint staff mission in Washington, the representation of the Department of Munitions and Supply in both capitals, and the offices abroad of the wartime information, board. There has been a similar growtQ of specialized representation in Ottawa, particularly in the case of the United Kingdom and the United States. On the military side, I need scarcely refer to the work performed in England by General McNaughton and by the overesas headquarters of the three armed services.
Before the United States entered the war we had supplemented our methods for considering problems of common interest by the creation of a series of joint advisory bodies dealing with the defence of North America, with raw materials, with economic coordination. and with war production. To these a joint committee on agriculture has recently been added. These committees and bodies supplement but do not replace the normal methods of consultation.
Shortly after Pearl Harbor, in order to secure more rapid cooperation between the war efforts of the United States and the United Kingdom, a group of combined agencies was established. These agencies are:
1.	The combined chiefs of staff, meeting continuously in Washington, composed of the United States chiefs of staff and representatives of the British chiefs of staff;
2.	The munitions assignments boards, meeting in Washington and in London, to allocate finished war materials on strategic grounds as they become ready for delivery;
3.	The shipping adjustment boards, also meeting in Washington and in London, to regulate the pools of shipping controlled by the United States and the United Kingdom; and
4.	The combined raw materials board, meeting in Washington, charged with the duty of planning the most effective use of raw materials. There were later added two further boards, both meeting in Washington;
5.	The combined food board, and
6.	The combined production resources board.
With one exception these bodies are composed of representatives only of the United States and the United Kingdom and their chief duty is to make recommendations to these two governments in the light of the joint study of the problems before them. They are war bodies formed for special purposes to facilitate the rapid taking of decisions on matters vital to the conduct of the war.
It is essential that the high strategy of the war should be discussed by a small group in conditions of the most absolute secrecy. To avoid giving aid to our enemies, a degree of secrecy, which would be intolerable in times of peace, must surround the taking of decisions, not only on strategy but on almost every aspect of war direction. The recommendations of the combined boards frequently concern governments other than the United States and the United Kingdom. When Canadian action is required to give effect to their recommendations, these recommendations are referred to Canada for approval. The government has sought, with a considerable measure of success, to ensure that in framing their recommendations the combined boards should give the fullest consideration to the position and resources of Canada.
A Canadian joint staff mission has offices in the building which houses the combined chiefs of staff, and it is represented at discussions of direct concern to Canada. We have developed special methods of liaison with each of the combined boards. In the case of the combined food board, for example, a representative of the Canadian government participates as a full member on all the commodity subcommittees.
On one board, the combined production and resources board, Canada is represented by a full member. The Minister of Munitions and

Supply (Mr. Howe) is a member of this board. The board, by the way, as hon. members are aware, is meeting in Ottawa this morning.
I have outlined the chief agencies that have been established for the direction of the war effort. The government hopes that it will be found possible to have a broader basis given to some of these bodies.
Turning now to the planning of the settlement, I have said on previous occasions in this house that informal and exploratory discussions about international aspects of the settlement were constantly taking place, and that Canadian experts and officials were participating in these discussions. On matters as complex as methods for stabilizing currencies, it is obvious that there must be many preliminary talks between experts from many countries before plans can be framed for the consideration of governments. Canadian officials have participated in such talks in London and in Washington. These meetings are supplemented by the constant exchange of information through the usual inter-governmental channels. As the end of the war comes closer, such meetings will grow in number. As plans are framed, they are likely to become the subject of more formal conferences at which most, if not all, of the united nations will be represented.
The first of such conferences-the united nations conference on food and agriculture- has already been held at Hot Springs, Virginia. Hon. members will recall that on June 14, in tabling the final act of this conference, I made a statement on the general work of the conference and the programme for future action. A further united nations conference to consider the international organization of relief in the immediate postwar period will be held later in the present year.
Other meetings will follow as the preliminary discussions complete the preparatory work on each major subject for international agreement. I cannot yet indicate exactly what these subjects will be. Doubtless among them will be included the distressing and baffling problem of refugees, which -has lately been discussed at a meeting in Bermuda between representatives of the United States and the United Kingdom. I shall speak of this problem in a moment.
It is too early for me to attempt even a shadowy outline of the form of the international settlement, political and economic, which may follow the ending of hostilities. It may be useful, however, to say a word

about one of its aspects. The strong bonds which have linked the united nations into a working model of cooperation must be strengthened and developed for even greater use in the years of peace. It is perhaps an axiom of war that during actual hostilities methods must be improvised-, secrecy must be observed, attention -must be concentrated on victory. The time is approaching, however, when even before victory is won the concept of the united nations will have to be embodied in some form of international organization. On the one hand, authority in international affairs must not be concentrated exclusively in the -largest powers. On the other, authority cannot be divided equally among all the thirty or more sovereign states that comprise the united nations, or all effective authority will disappear. A number of new international institutions are likely to be set up as a result of the war. In the view of the government, effective representations on these bodies should neither 'be restricted to the largest states nor necessarily extended to all states. Representation should be determined on a functional basis which will admit to full membership those countries, large or small, which have the greatest contribution to make to the particular object in question. In the -world there are over sixty sovereign states. If they all have a nominally equal voice in international decisions, no effective decisions are likely to be taken. Some compromise must be found between 'the theoretical equality of states and the practical necessity of limiting representation on international bodies to a workable number. That compromise can be discovered, especially in economic matters, by the adoption of the functional principle of representation. That principle, in turn, is likely to find many new expressions in the gigantic task of liberation, restoration and reconstruction.
I shall now make a statement on the policy of the government with respect to refugees from Europe. Only the most callous could contemplate with indifference the situation of most of those unfortunates who, since Hitler's assumption of power, have been driven from their homes. Among them are to be found members of nearly every nationality and creed under the sun. They have been scattered far and wide. Most of them, however, including those whose sufferings are greatest, are still contained within the ring of territories held by the axis armies. For them, except perhaps for a tiny number who

Sup-ply-External Affairs-War Situation
may by subterfuge or stealth cross the axis-held frontiers to neighbouring neutral countries, the only escape from persecution lies in the victory of the armies of the united nations.
Inside German dominated Europe terrible things are happening, but the lash has fallen on the backs of the Jews more heavily than on any other group or race. Last December, the allied governments in London, in conjunction with the United Kingdom and the United States, issued a declaration denouncing the ruthless German policy of extermination of the Jewish people under their control and promising retribution. The government of Canada was glad immediately to associate itself with this declaration. There is, unfortunately, abundant evidence that there has been no change during the last six months. Indeed, in eastern Europe especially, the signs are that the treatment of the Jews has grown even more pitiless, and Jews from the western European territories under German control have been moved eastwards to share the fate of those from central and eastern Europe.
There is nothing that the allied governments can do to save these hapless people except to win the war as quickly and as completely as possible. They cannot be removed from axis territory. Efforts to aid them, even if aid was feasible, would prolong their agony if these efforts were to prolong the war. It was agreed, at the recent Bermuda conference between officials of the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom, that no negotiations could be undertaken with Hitler, since his entire record has left no doubt that he would only agree to such solutions as would be of direct aid to the axis war aims. It was also agreed that nothing could be recommended that would interfere or delay the war effort of the united nations.
This Bermuda conference, however, has made a number of recommendations for the purpose of assisting those refugees who have already managed to penetrate through the axis ring to neutral countries. While victory alone can reach the central core of the refugee problem, it is not by any means beyond the power of the united nations to aid those who have escaped but have not yet found a safe asylum until peace is restored. I cannot give the house details either of the number of refugees in various neutral and allied territories or of the proposals-now accepted by the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom -which were recommended by the Bermuda
conference. The delegations agreed that the details of their deliberations must be regarded as confidential so long as a knowledge of their recommendations would be of aid or comfort to our enemies or might adversely affect the refugees whom all are trying to aid. The universal problem of shipping was also recognized at the conference as of the utmost urgency and it was agreed there that any plan that looked to the diverting of allied shipping from the war effort, to remove or care for refugees, would present considerations of a military character which would disclose almost insuperable difficulties.

Refugees who have -escaped into Spain, Portugal, the middle east, and Africa, but have not yet found a safe resting place, can, if shipping is available, be moved to places where they can remain until peace is restored. This group includes many thousands of many races: Poles and Frenchmen, Czechs, Greeks and Yugoslavs, as well as Jews.
All that I can say about the decisions at Bermuda is to quote as follows from' the statement issued after the conference:
The conference was able to recommend measures both for removing refugees from neutral countries and, in those cases, where such removal was not possible, for giving assurances of international cooperation in the future of the refugee problem so far as it affected them.
It also recommended a number of temporary refugee havens to which refugees could be transported and maintained if and when shipping should become available. At least one such movement has been effected.

The Bermuda conference also made certain recommendations of a more general character. The refugee problem is essentially an internaticAial one, which can only be solved by cooperative effort. The conference recommended that the inter-governmental committee on refugees, which was established at the Evian meeting of 1938, should be reconstituted with increased authority, larger membership and greater financial resources. The Canadian government will be glad to play its part in giving effect to this recommendation. The conference also recommended, in order to allay the anxiety especially of neutral European countries, that the united nations should in a declaration provide for the repatriation of refugees to their own lands at the end of the war. The conference adopted other proposals designed to. make it easier for neutral countries to maintain the refugees in their territories whose removal could not be arranged. The Canadian government has not yet been asked to assist in giving effect to the proposals framed at Bermuda, but it will be glad to play its full part as soon as these proposals are presented to the united nations. This would include participation in the revised and strengthened inter-governmental committee, and also the reception in Canada until peace is restored of a number of refugees in addition to those already within the country.
I cannot state how many additional refugees Canada will be prepared to receive. This depends on many factors not within the control of the Canadian government. The dispersion of refugees now in neutral European countries, and the reception of those who may hereafter escape from axis territories, must be conducted under international auspices, with consideration given to the possibilities of transport, of repatriation at the end of the war, of uniting families and of useful employment in the war industries. Considerations of security must be carefully weighed in individual cases. A declaration such as the government has been urged to make, that Canada would receive all refugees from axis territory who could reach her shores, would be an invitation to the German government to distribute in this manner their spies and secret agents.
There is outstanding an offer of the Canadian government made last autumn to receive for the duration of the war up to 1.000 Jewish children then in unoccupied France and separated from their parents. The care and maintenance of these children was guaranteed through the Canadian Jewish congress under conditions generally similar to those applied
[Mr. Mackenzie King.)
to children evacuated from the British isles in 1940 under the government scheme. Before effect could be given to this offer, the Germans occupied the whole of France. The offer, however, is still valid. If arrangements can be made through neutral countries or the intergovernmental committee for the departure of *these children from France, we shall gladly accord them admission to Canada.
We already have in Canada a. very considerable refugee population. Many of those here have been admitted' for permanent residence in accordance with the provisions of the Immigration Act and regulations. Others have been granted asylum for the duration of the war only, and it is to this latter group *that I wish now to refer for a moment. There are doubtless among them many who would be glad to make their permanent homes in Canada, including some who have come from the British isles and some from countries of continental Europe. While the government can give no general undertaking that all who wish to stay will be granted the right to reside permanently in Canada, individual applications for permission to remain in this country after the war will be given full and sympathetic consideration.
It is hard to say how many refugees from Europe have been admitted to Canada since Hitler's rise to power. In our immigration statistics there is no category of entrants who are recorded as refugees. My impression is that those who criticize what has been done, and accuse the government of inertia and inhumanity, are often not fully cognizant of the facts. In the years 1933-42, nine thousand persons were admitted as immigrants to Canada by special orders in council, and most of them were European refugees. In addition, shortly before the war, 300 families and a substantial number of single men from the Sudeten area were admitted for agricultural settlement in western Canada, and hundreds of other agricultural refugees from central Europe were also admitted during that period. The total immigration from Europe, between April 1, 1933, and March 31. 1942, was 39,000, the bulk of whom were refugees. All these entered Canada for permanent residence.
I cannot even give an approximate figure of those admitted temporarily, as the records do not exist. All I can say is that these amount to several thousands, not including nearly 8.000 women and children who have been evacuated from the British isles since the spring of 1940. We have released also, under temporary status in Canada, about 900 persons of German and Austrian citizenship, who

Supply-External Affairs-War Situation
were transferred to Canada in July 1940 by the United Kingdom government. In addition we have received several hundred Polish and Czech technicians to work in our war industries. Quite apart from all these groups I should mention the many thousand prisoners of war who have been transferred to Canada for safe custody; while they are in no way refugees they constitute nevertheless a drain on our supplies and resources and their presence here has made it easier for refugees to be accommodated in African and Middle East territories under allied control.
We have not, of course, done all that we could have done and perhaps we have not done all that we should have done. Our record, however, is better than it is frequently made out to be and I think that it will stand comparison with the records of other parts of the British commonwealth and of the United States.
Since the outbreak of war Canada's diplomatic representation has been greatly extended. In September, 1939, Canada had, in addition to the long-established office of the High Commissioner in London, legations in the United States, France, Japan, and in Belgium and the Netherlands, as well as the office of the permanent delegate to the League of Nations. Since that time the legations in Paris, Tokyo, Brussels and the Hague and the office in Geneva have been closed. But in the interval, fourteen new offices abroad have been established. Of these, five represent the appointment of high commissioners within the British commonwealth, to Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland and Newfoundland. Five are of new legations, to U.S.S.R. and China, and in South America to Brazil, Argentine and Chile. In addition, one minister has been accredited to seven of the allied governments established during the war in London: Belgium, the Netherlands, Poland, Norway, Yugoslavia, Greece and Czechoslovakia. All of the countries I have mentioned are represented in Ottawa by ministers, high commissioners or accredited representatives as the case may be.
Consular officers of Canada are serving in Greenland, and in St. Pierre and Miquelon. Most recently, with the appointment of a consul-general to New York, the first separate consular establishment in the United States has been opened.
The supervisory commission of the League of Nations still meets, though not at Geneva, and there is a Canadian representative on this continuing body. An important part of the league, the International Labour Organization, has, since 1940, had its headquarters at Montreal.
All of these formal relationships speak of the developing importance of Canada in the world community. The fortunes of war-or perhaps something more than the fortunes- have brought to Canada valiant men and women of many nations: sovereigns, prime ministers, foreign ministers and officers of state; chiefs of staff and ranking officers of armies, navies and air forces of many lands.
The stature of nationhood which Canada has reached-I mean the position of Canada as a world power-has been reached, not on material grounds alone, though Canada's contributions to mutual aid have been impressive by any standard. Neither does it owe its emergence to political considerations. It has arisen, I believe, from our recognition of the needs of humanity. Our conception of nationhood rejects, as it must always reject, any attachment to ideas which are non-democratic, or to usages which would constitute the negation of free institutions and the untrammelled expression of the free souls of free men. It is something which speaks not simply for to-day, or next month, or the year after next, but for all the future of Canada.

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity that has been afforded the House of Commons" during the present session to discuss Canada's foreign policy, and I think that is to be regretted. Questions of foreign policy are daily becoming of greater importance to Canada. They are probably the most vital questions this house can face in any of its sessions. Therefore I deprecate greatly the practice of the government in postponing each session the discussion of foreign policy, and then setting aside a very short time for that purpose.
It has always seemed to me that it would be very helpful if we were to have set up in this house a committee to be known as a foreign affairs committee, or one at any rate which would deal with questions of foreign affairs. For that matter there might also be a similar committee set up in the senate. I am confident that if this step were taken it would mean that the government of the day would get help in settling problems having to do with foreign affairs. It would also mean that members of both the Senate and the House of Commons would be far better informed on foreign questions, and it would help the Canadian people to get a better grasp of the. different problems.
At the present time Canadians are given very little leadership by this parliament in connection with foreign affairs and yet the foreign policy of any country must be based upon the beliefs and wishes of its people.
Supply-External Affairs

Before the war Canada's foreign policy might be summed up as, first of all, friendliness to all nations. With that policy no one can quarrel, although at times it was carried to an absurd length-for example with Germany and with Japan. Hon. members who were in the last House of Commons, the last parliament, will remember how this government allowed scrap iron to be shipped out to Japan, even when it was obvious to everyone that it was only a matter of time before Japan would be at war with the British commonwealth and with the United States. Friendliness in foreign affairs can very easily go so far as to become a policy of hiding your head in the sand.
Then, the second branch of Canada's foreign policy before the war was that we had no commitments to anyone-either to Great Britain, to any of the other members of the commonwealth, to the United States or any other nation. Time and again both in the house and on the hustings members of the government stated that policy-that Canada had no commitments. And they put it in this way, that Canada could be informed by Great Britain of what was going on, but she could not be consulted, the implication being that if she were consulted she would be under some obligation, and Canada felt that she should be under no obligation to Great Britain or to anyone else.
Now, that was the announced policy. In actual fact it was not the policy. One has only to refer to the report of the imperial conference held in London in 1937 to learn that at that time and at that conference the main topics of discussion were foreign affairs and defence. Quite extensive plans were made for the empire, for the commonwealth, to have a common policy in foreign affairs, and also for the defence of the commonwealth as a unit. But the government did not see fit to explain that to the Canadian people. And I do suggest for the future-unfortunately it is too late now to do anything about the past -it would have been better if the government had come right out in the open and said, "The nations of the British commonwealth propose to stand together, war or no war. War or no war we stand together as a British family; and let the rest of the world take notice accordingly." That is the only fair way to treat the Canadian people. Hearing this talk of a no-commitment policy, and not knowing where they stood, there was utter confusion from one end of Canada to the other with regard to Canada's foreign policy. I repeat it would have been far better for the Canadian people if they had been told by their government that the British family intended to stand together as one, and that Canada was with the rest of the family.

Perhaps the most humiliating situation in which Canada was placed as a result of this no-commitment policy was on July 1, 1938, Canada's birthday, when those of us who were in the last parliament had to sit in the house and hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) say that he was unwilling to have Great Britain set up schools in Canada for the training of her airmen, because that would be the equivalent of setting up a foreign military station in this land.

May I say a word with respect to the idea of having the imperial air force set up flying schools in Canada to train their pilots; in short, a military station put down in Canada, owned, maintained and operated by the imperial government for imperial purposes. The Prime Minister goes on to say:
Such domestic ownership, maintenance and control of all military stations and personnel is one of the really indispensable hall marks of national sovereign self-government and an indispensable basis for friendly and effective

cooperation between the governments of Canada and those of other parts of the British commonwealth of nations, including the government of the United Kingdom.

Mr. Bennett:	This is not a military force
but a training force.

My reference was with regard to the idea of having the imperial air force set up a flying school somewhere in Canada to train their flying pilots. In short, a military station to be put down in Canada, owned, maintained and operated by the imperial government for imperial purposes.
Mr. Bennett: Not for imperial purposes.

speechtext:
If the Prime Minister
wishes to explain his words he will have an opportunity to do so.
The third branch of Canada's foreign policy before the war was that there was great emphasis placed at all times upon our independence and our equality of status. It was claimed that Canada was a nation by reason of the imperial conference of 1926 and of the Balfour declaration and the statute of Westminster which followed. Actually Canada became a nation because of the fighting of the Canadian corps in the last war. Those were the three branches of Canada's foreign policy before the war- friendliness, no commitments, and emphasis on equality of status.
Now after four years of war presumably Canada still has a policy of friendliness, but I believe the Canadian government no longer follows the policy of no commitments. We have commitments in every direction, and quite properly so. The stage of no commitments has long since passed. But the Canadian government has not yet given up the third branch of its foreign policy, which, as I have said, is to place great stress on equality of status. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), on March 19 of this year, outlined Canada's foreign policy, and by the way be did it then much more fully than
he has done to-day. He read the Balfour declaration and ended his speech with these words:
In all our relations with other parts of the empire and with other countries, so far as the present administration is concerned, we intend to stand on the ground of a status of our own equal to that of each and all of the self-governing communities-the dominions and the United Kingdom included.
No one either inside of Canada or outside of Canada is questioning Canada's equality of status or Canada's independence, and the government in making a declaration of policy of this type is setting up a straw man simply to knock him down. In these days, in the fourth year of the war and approaching the fifth year, Canada needs something far more up to date and far more realistic in the line of foreign policy. We are living in a different world from that of 1939. There have been great developments as a result of the war. I need not list them, but there have been developments, for instance, in the way of raising men for the armed forces, in the production of manufactured goods, in the pror duction of food, and other developments so great -that the Prime Minister the other day, on July 1, another of Canada's birthdays, boasted in this fashion, as found at page 4226 of Hansard:
In the course of the present war, we have seen Canada emerge from nationhood into a position generally recognized as that of a world power.
Canada a world power! Those are striking words and thought-provoking words for every man and woman in- Canada, and they can be made a fact. But they will never be made a fact with a Canadian foreign policy that emphasizes only friendliness for all and equality of status with the other British nations. That does not go far enough. Something more is required if Canada is to be a world power. A foreign policy is required that will give the Canadian people a vision of their nation taking a stand on world questions as they arise, and not simply waiting outside the door for some of the larger nations to hand out a decision. Canada herself must take a stand on world questions as they arise. Secondly, a vision of Canada boldly asking for the sort of world that Canadians believe in as individuals. Thirdly, Canada must be willing to assume her fair share of responsibilities, of whatever burdens there may be entailed in order that a better world may be developed after this war.
If the Canadian people catch this vision of Canada as a world power taking the lead in making a better world, they will so build this nation and develop Canada-and after
Supply'-External Affairs

all it is the people who develop a nation, not the government-that she will become such a world power.
The foreign policy announced by the Prime Minister is too much wrapped up in a blanket of words, which is one of the great failings of the Prime Minister in practically all his announcements, and it is qualified by too many provisos. Canadians must have a foreign policy that is straightforward and easily understood by all. To-day I make bold to suggest certain broad principles for a Canadian foreign policy and to ask the government to give them the most serious consideration.
The first principle I enunciate is this, that the Canadian government should make it known to the Canadian people that this nation has finished forever with a policy of no commitments, with a policy, in other words, of isolation. It must be clear now to the most stupid person in the civilized world that no nation can stand alone. Let Canada be prepared' to stand with all the other nations who are seeking 'to build a better world.
The second principle is that Canada will accept her full share of responsibility for maintaining law and order beyond her own boundaries. That may mean that Canada must provide an air force for the post-war period, that she must provide troops, that she must provide naval forces for the maintenance of law and order beyondi the 'boundaries of Canada. We must be prepared to take our share in maintaining order after the war. The United States is moving along this line. I was very much impressed by what is known as the Fulbright resolution, a resolution recently passed unanimously by the foreign affairs committee of the House of Representatives favouring-
-the creation of appropriate international machinery with power adequate to establish and maintain a just and lasting peace among the nations of the world and favouring participation by the United States therein.
That is a notable declaration by the United States House of Representatives, and a principle of that type could very well be adopted and enunciated by the Canadian parliament.
The third principle is this, that Canada intends to stay in the British family of nations, that Canada intends to develop within the British commonwealth. That will mean Canada standing as a world power at the side of Great Britain, perhaps a power with a larger population eventually than Great Britain; in my opinion, if this nation is given proper leadership, that will become the case in course of time. And it should be made clear that Canada believes that the

British family of nations should speak with one voice in foreign affairs. That is what the United States and the other nations of the world expect; -that is what the Canadian people want-make no mistake about it-and in the long run Canada's foreign policy will be what the man on the street wants it to be.
In recent years Canada has placed too much emphasis on status. It is like a man throwing out his chest and showing off what a big fellow he is. That is very clearly brought out in a pamphlet entitled "The British Commonwealth at War", by William Yandell Elliott and H. Duncan Hall, and published this year. At page 14 I read this:
The period in which the emphasis was laid by the British dominions upon status, rather than upon their common interests and their obligations as members of the British commonwealth, lasted for little more than fifteen years; it ended roughly in 1935, when the world began to be once more manifestly unsafe for small powers. The dominions which placed the most emphasis upon status were Canada, the most secure of all the dominions, and Eire and South Africa which, because some of their population had recently been at war with Britain, were under a deep psychological necessity to assert their independence. Australia and New Zealand, the most exposed to danger from war, the most British in the composition of their populations, the most free from memories of past friction with Britain, placed far less emphasis upon status and far more upon the sharing of mutual obligations with the other members of the commonwealth and the making of contributions to the common defence.
In the League of Nations we had1 the British commonwealth speaking with different voices. Other nations have never understood that, and they never will in the days that are to come. The fact of Canada declining to be consulted, Canada holding back, has resulted in Great Britain, which had to speak for herself, being taken in effect as speaking for the British commonwealth. From the statements of Mr. Eden, the British Foreign Secretary, in Washington when he was there this spring, it is clear that Great Britain does not like that; that she would like to have the commonwealth speaking as a unit. We find this press quotation in the papers of March 27 of this year from Washington, dealing with Mr. Eden's visit:
Here in Washington the Foreign Secretary has made no secret of his desire for further collaboration between the commonwealth on foreign policy or any other matter. He has made it clear that Britain claims no exclusive representation for the empire on the various combined organizations now set up and in the process of formation-and in fact would be willing to step down in turn to make room for the dominions to represent the commonwealth.

Supply-External Affairs
There is danger of a Big Four seUup in international affairs, with Canada one of the smaller nations waiting around outside. The Prime Minister this very morning has told us about the leading boards, and he has said that with the exception of one, on which our Minister of Munitions and Supply is a representative, all of them are United Kingdom-United States boards. Just the other day, on June 11, announcement was made that a relief agency had been formed of the united nations. Canada is vitally concerned with that relief agency because she will have to supply a large portion of the food and other materials. Yet we find in another press dispatch from Washington, dated June 10:
The real governing board, however, will be the central committee consisting of representatives of the big four, Britain, the United States, Russia and China.
Although the draft agreement does not suggest Canada for membership on the central committee, despite the fact that Canada, next to the United States, will provide more relief food than any other country, there is one position of major importance that would seem to be ideally suited to Canada's unique position. That is the chairmanship of the supplies committee.
Andi then it goes on:
It may develop that Canada will be selected at the Washington conference for this role, having been left off the central committee.
If Canada insists on taking her part in the councils of the nations as a wholly autonomous, independent unit of the British commonwealth, showing that the commonwealth has no common foreign policy, she can expect nothing but to end up in the position in which she has ended up on so many of these committees. She can expect at best a minor and an indirect voice in such councils. The tragic feature of that policy is that the result will be that Canada will develop a small nation complex and will never be anything but a small state.
I suggest to hon. members that it would be far better for Canada to develop within the British commonwealth, thereby greatly strengthening it, thereby giving the commonwealth a far stronger voice in world affairs, and in fact thereby making the commonwealth the basis of a broader world order. The British commonwealth needs Canada. It needs Canada just as much as Canada needs the other nations of the commonwealth. Canada is the keystone of the British empire. We are an Atlantic power, a Pacific power, an American power, and now, with the development of aeroplanes, we are an Arctic power. I would impress upon the Prime Minister that Canada is now the keystone of the British empire and that we should plan with that thought in mind.
Take for example the British commonwealth air training plan. What a wonderful thing that has been. It shows what can be done when the nations of the British commonwealth make up their minds to really work together. We can carry out plans of that type with regard to our air development in the post-war days. I do not intend to go any further into that, because the subject will be dealt with by my colleague the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I am sure that what our lads who are serving in every part of the globe would insist upon, if they could be here, would be that Canada shall develop as a great nation within the British commonwealth. After all, they are the Canadians who are really making Canada a world power-not those of us who are here at home.
The fourth principle of Canada's foreign policy should be that the British commonwealth and the United States are indispensable to one another and must be in alliance for all time. Let us face that fact and tell the rest of the world it is what we believe. There has been no war between those two groups of British peoples for over 128 years. That is a significant fact; it shows that our interests are parallel; had it not been so there would have been war between the peoples long since.
This whole question of the relationship between the British commonwealth and the United States is very clearly expressed in a book by Walter Lippmann, which has been published this last month, entitled " U. S. Foreign Policy: Shield of the Republic." It is a small book, which it would repay any hon. member to read, because it applies not only to United States foreign policy, but also to Canadian foreign policy. At page 127 Mr. Lippmann says:
Is it not undeniable that American commitments in the Atlantic and the Pacific dictate the need for an alliance with the British commonwealth of nations and with the empire? ... It is better to proclaim frankly that the alliance is necessary, and then to demonstrate the need for it to the common sense of the British, the Canadian, and the American people.
I suggest to hon. members that that is good advice as well for Canadians.
The fifth principle is this, that Canada, as an American nation and a nation which has always been friendly with all other nations of this hemisphere, should be an active member of the Pan-American Union, it being understood of course that we are not to be taken thereby as weakening our connection with the British commonwealth of nations. Just a few days ago, on June 28, the Prime Minister tabled an inter-American radio agreement,
Supply-External Affairs

and it is strange to find that it was an agreement signed in Chile on January 26, 1940, over three years ago. Canada was not present at the negotiations and is not really a party to the agreement, but Canada adhered to the agreement on the 8th of May, 1943. This shows the ridiculous position in which we are placed in our dealings with other nations of this hemisphere. I repeat that we should become an active member of the Pan-American Union.
The sixth and final .principle is this, that Canada should promote the closest cooperation with Russia, China, and the other united nations, and that Canada hopes eventually to see established a world organization which will include all nations. I would point out Canada's position with regard to Russia. The development of the aeroplane has made Russia our neighbour over the north pole; we have had Russian aviators flying here by that route; we are also close neighbours by way of Alaska; and we must cooperate with that great nation. China will be a great field for trade after the war and that is of particular interest to those Canadians who live on the Pacific slope, and I repeat that Canada should promote the closest cooperation with her.
These are the six principles I place before the Prime Minister and the house for consideration. There may be others that are equally important, and I hope that members will bring forward suggestions for Canada's foreign policy. These principles are clear; I believe they are sound; and they are based on what is Canada's own interest. In the last analysis that must be the basis for the foreign policy of any nation-whether it is in the interests of the people of that nation.
In conclusion, for Canada this is a turning point. We are at a turning point in the history of this country. Either we go on from here and become a real world power, or we develop a small-nation complex; and now is the time to place before the Canadian people a vision of what this wonderful nation of ours can be.

This is the first opportunity this session which the house has had of discussing external affairs. I was hoping that opportunities might have been found to enable us to go into the question of external affairs before reaching this stage of our proceedings. On March 19, as reported at page 1398 of Hansard, I said to the Prime Minister:
I think it would be of value if at an early day the Prime Minister would call an item in his estimates so that there might be a discussion of Canada's external affairs. It would enable us to arrive at a clearer understanding of some of the things, which, as he suggests, may becloud the issue.
The report goes on:
Mr. Mackenzie King:	I am anxious that
the house shall get on with its business as rapidly as possible. Before we take up any new subject for discussion we should conclude with the matters in hand.
Mr. Coldwell: I agree. I meant not to leave it until the dying days of the session.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I shall undertake with pleasure to see that matters of foreign policy are discussed before that time.
That was during the budget debate. Since then other departments have gone into supply and have had some of their estimates discussed, but external affairs has been left until the dying days of the session, when the house is tired and when we are faced with a great deal of unfinished business. To my mind this is one of the most important debates in the course of the session. Throughout the years we have not had that consideration of external affairs that should have been given by this parliament, and much of what the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) said this morning, a great deal of his criticism, is due to the fact that this house has not given sufficient attention to questions of external policy and external affairs.

I believe I have the floor. This is the 107th day of the session. It is all very well for the Prime Minister to say that there is a committee and that any hon. member may request that it be called; but, as he well knows, members of the house usually wait for some move from the government or from the government side of the house to encourage the calling of such a committee. But even that does not excuse the Prime Minister, as Minister for External Affairs, for leaving this important matter until the 107th day of this session. I know that the Prime Minister is busy. I know that he has many weighty affairs to which he must given his attention, and I was therefore surprised, when the assistants to the various ministers were appointed, that no assistant was appointed to the Prime Minister in his capacity as Minister for External Affairs. It seemed to me that if there was one place where assistance was necessary it was in that particular department, and I had hoped that some additional attention would be given to external affairs by the appointment of an assistant.
There are a good many things I desire to say in connection with this debate, but perhaps, in order to put myself in the frame of mind in which I can discuss these matters with rather more careful consideration, and since I want to deal with something which is a little unpleasant, I may observe by way of preface that I have always refrained from making personal attacks. I think every member of the house will give me credit for that. It is against my nature and my way of doing things to make personal attacks. On May 14 I had occasion to refer to one of our ministers, the minister at Washington, Mr. McCarthy, and I made certain criticisms to which I shall allude in a moment. On May 17 the Prime Minister rose in the house and gave me something of a castigation for, to use his own words, "making innuendoes of a character unworthy" of myself, and making, as he said, all kinds of irresponsible representations regarding the minister at Washington. Now the only irresponsible statement made in that regard was a statement by the Prime Minister when he said:
I am prepared to support all the representations made by Mr. McCarthy in the statement he has presented here.
Shortly after that statement, within a week of raising the matter in the house, I was in Washington. Mr. McCarthy sent me an invitation to visit him. I visited him, and on that

I regard this war, particularly since the fall of France and the retreat from Dunkirk, not as an ordinary war, a war for territory-no; a war for commerce-no; a war for imperial power-no; but, if I may use the term strictly in its dictionary sense, as a part of a great revolutionary struggle that has been going on all over the world for some time, and which can only culminate in the setting up all over the world of democratic governments that are strictly responsible to and controlled by the people of the various countries of the world. Because I believe that, I wonder why it is that favour has been shown to persons who have not followed out policies in accord with the general trend of events.
We know, for example, it is said of General de Gaulle that he is a difficult man to get along with. Well, we do know, of course, that after the fall of France de Gaulle was the only French general of prominence who allied himself, and those who followed him, with our side. We know also that de Gaulle has become the symbol of the underground movement of resistance in France, and the symbol of that democratic power which the people of suffering France hope will emerge when the united nations are victorious. Consequently one finds it very difficult indeed to follow what has been done in North Africa and elsewhere with any degree of optimism for the future.
I am certain that the peoples who are suffering in Europe are not suffering because they wish to reestablish the kind of Europe that was known before this great catastrophe came upon the world. Therefore it is alarming to many people to see the support accorded, particularly by our great neighbour to the south, to persons such as those to whom I have just alluded. Even to-day, while we are glad to welcome General Giraud to North America, we wonder why some time ago General de Gaulle was not accorded a similar spontaneous and hearty invitation or welcome to this part of the world.
This morning I was glad to hear the hon. member for Vancouver South say that he thought the time had come when we should, if an opportunity offers, unite ourselves with the Pan-American Union. I think that would be a forward step. Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes that are left to me there are one or two matters with which I want to deal very briefly. There are so many topics that it is difficult to pick and choose between them in a discussion of external affairs. I do, however, wish to say that Canada should be considering very carefully future policy and our relations with the world at large in regard to that policy. We cannot live apart from other nations, and it seems to me that for a country like Canada the policy we should pursue is that of the greatest possible cooperation with countries with like aims and ideals to our own. There can be no security for a small nation apart from some form of collective security. We remain close to the British commonwealth of nations because to many of us this commonwealth of free self-governing nations is perhaps the promise of better things to come in the future of the world, when nations equal in status will be able to formulate policies in cooperation with one another for the establishment of international justice and the enforcement of international law and order, and in. such a community of nations Canada should play its proper part.
This morning I was discussing matters in connection with one of our legations. In my opinion Canada ought to be represented as widely as possible in the capitals of the countries with which we are in the closest contact.
I am glad that the government has adopted the policy of exchanging representatives with a good many nations. I should like to see that policy expanded. I know that there has been some discussion with the republic of Mexico. It seems to me that Mexico, as another north American nation, ought to be in contact with us in a regular and diplomatic manner.
Of those who represent us in such places I would like to say that the government should endeavour to establish within the Department of External Affairs a system of training and promotion of men most suitable to represent Canada abroad. I do not regard it as either wise or good that our representatives in foreign countries should have to be rich men. Of that kind of representation one is critical, and one should not be critical of a man representing Canada merely because he is rich. A qualification for the representation of Canada abroad ought not to be that a man has a large private income. Those of us who visited the legation in Washington the other day were quite well aware of the fact that it would be very difficult indeed for a civil servant on the salary and allowances we provide to keep up the almost palatial quarters that we have in the city of Washington. I am of the opinion that we should have modest quarters, where a man living on the salary and emoluments provided by the government of Canada would have sufficient to do what is expected of him as the representative of this nation abroad. I do think we should be represented in the capitals of countries with which we are in closest contact, both politically and commercially, and that of course applies particularly at the moment to the countries of South America.
There are other matters which I should like to discuss, but since my time has expired I do not propose to enter upon another topic which would require more than the few moments of discussion that I am able to give to it. Suffice it to say that I am firmly of the opinion that we in this'-house must take a much deeper interest in the international relationships of our country than we have done in the past. The events which led up to the great war were very largely events over which we had no control and with which we had no close contact, and step by step we found that a government whose policies we followed deserted principles of collective security to which we should have tried to adhere closely. Finally the world went up again in flames. It seems to me that it is the duty of representatives of the people in every parliament and every legislature in the world to consider

Mr. Chairman, with the closing remarks of the speaker who has immediately preceded me I think everyone in the house and in the country and perhaps in the world at large will be wholly in accord. It is so easy to speak about beautiful things that all people desire, but so difficult to make it clear how those beautiful things are to be achieved. It is easy enough to speak of collective security, for example, but when it comes to deciding with whom you are going to collect, and upon what basis you are going to collect, the problem is not nearly so simple. I surely agree, as I have already indicated, with the closing words of the previous speaker, but I am not sure that he and I would agree very much further, especially when the question arose as to how we proposed to achieve the objects we all desire.
May I turn now for a moment to a consideration of the Prime Minister's speech. The Prime Minister, I believe, is the most successful man on the earth, so far as I know, in saying beautiful things that have no meaning at all. I think everyone agrees with everything the man says. But nobody ever knows just what he means by what he says. His speech to-day was no exception. At every point where it became necessary to know just what he had in mind, his thoughts were veiled behind beautiful tapestries which hid his real thoughts from us.
I shall endeavour to be specific. Probably I am sometimes a bit too specific, because I find nearly everyone disagreeing with me. That tends to occur when one is specific and says exactly what he means.
I am going to deal with foreign affairs under three main headings; for one has to narrow the compass of his thoughts in order to get anywhere. I shall deal first with the question of international relations as the members of our party look upon international relations. We believe that primarily the first and most important thing for any nation to do is to set its own house in order, and we insist that our nation shall be left free and untrammelled from external restrictions either by contract or by implication of contract, to exercise her complete sovereignty in putting her house in order. Our greatest anxiety as we face the future and listen to the beautiful outbursts of our Prime Minister

and a good many other statesmen to-day is that they are not really cognizant of all the powers which this country needs to retain in order to be able to set her own house in order. We believe that if the purchasing power within the country of Canada is raised to the right level, and that if we have fair prices so that we can have plenty for all; if we can have a rich and varied industrial development which will enable us to produce to the highest degree the needs of Canada, we shall be on our way to putting our own house in order; and that unless we have all these things we shall not be on our way to putting our own house in order. We believe too that if we provide as far as possible for our own needs, thereby avoiding the obligation of trading unnecessarily, we shall place our feet on the solid rock of substantial reality which will enable us to stand against the storms of time.
Beyond producing our own needs in Canada it will be essential that we develop our resources to a degree which will enable us to help our neighbours to obtain their needs. If I may cite as an example one of the nations with whom we are at war, all hon. members realize that Japan is not bountifully endowed by nature as is Canada. I think we realized that when we granted Japan special privileges in our fishing waters. When the war is over and we shall have beaten Japan to her knees, and further than that, the problem will arise, how are we going to build up a world in which the Japanese not yet born will be able to live and have as good a chance as the Canadians who are not yet born? We must face that problem fairly and squarely; if we do not, we shall betray the responsibilities which rest inevitably upon us in the position of trust in which our fellow countrymen have placed us.
Canadian production should make allowance not only for supplying Canada with all She needs, but for supplying Japan, and other nations less bountifully and fortunately endowed than we, with a certain amount of what they need in order that their standard of living may be what it ought to be in a world of abundance, a world as happy as ours should be if only we learned how to manage it.
Up to the present time practically everyone in Canada and the United States, and in fact all these united nations which are working together, has thought only of producing goods which he hoped to sell to somebody else, regardless of whether the somebody else wanted the goods, regardless of whether the sale would injure some other nation. We must change our outlook entirely with respect

Supply-External Affairs
to this matter. Our aim must not be to produce the goods which we think we can crowd into other people's markets to their advantage or not, to the disadvantage of other nations or not; we must produce the goods which other nations need and which they will request from us. This is an extremely important matter. If we produce goods to obtrude them into the world's markets, we shall be encouraging an international trade competition which will result in trade rivalry, which will lead to trade war, which will bring about military war as sure as we are all sitting here in this house, just as it resulted in the war in which we are now engaged. For one of the major causes of war is commercial rivalry, trade war. If we are wise we shall build for a future in which trade wars will be unnecessary. True, that will require the application of a number of principles with which very few people in this house and in this country are familiar. There will have to be a new order established, and perforce new principles must underlie that new order.
So that the members of my party take the stand, first of all, that Canada must show the world, by putting her own house in order, that a people with the economic security and democratic freedom which our people can be brought to enjoy will not covet their neighbour's possessions, that they will be happy, not disposed to risk war, not disposed to prepare for war.
Much has been said of the fact that the United States and Canada have lived together over a hundred years without having any fortifications along their border. Not much is said of the fact that neither one of these nations needed anything the other nation had. In other words, the cause of war between the two nations had been in large measure removed. It might not have resulted so happily had conditions been otherwise. We believe that if we can enable nations like Germany after the war to have, first, security, and afterwards, a democratic freedom, they will not study war nor the making of war. We believe that Canada can be made to show, by setting her own house in order, that that is possible, and we believe that in order to enable Germany to be secure, too, there are several principles of international relations which should apply.
Canada should encourage trade with other countries of a reciprocal and mutually acceptable basis, avoiding cut-throat competition for foreign markets, which results in bitter commercial rivalry. As I said a minute ago, how to do that is the problem. May I say here that the Prime Minister has not indicated in
the slightest degree that he knows anything at all about how to do that, and I will challenge any hon. member on the Liberal side to indicate where the Prime Minister has shown that he knows how to do it. The coast is free; hon. members can rise and speak after I have finished.
In addition, Social Creditors advocate the principle that we exercise and maintain unimpaired, as a member of the British commonwealth, our sovereign authority to order our own affairs in accordance with the will of our people.
May I refer to one thing that was tabled in the house not very long ago. I do so to illustrate how that sovereign power could be destroyed without our realizing it. I refer to the little pamphlet which every member has received, "International Stabilization of Currencies." I have been told that Canada has submitted a plan of her own, or at least she is preparing a plan of her own for submission, which, I take it, indicates that Canada is not satisfied with either of the plans advanced in this pamphlet, namely the Keynes plan and the Morgenthau plan. If Canada has rejected these two plans and has a plan of her own, I say that is an exceedingly complimentary thing to the dominion. For these two plans are pernicious in a high degree.
