I too am interested to know and possibly the Prime Minister will tell us whether Canada is preparing to accept either of the plans to which I have referred. If so, then Canada is preparing to yield her sovereignty in a way which will prevent her from ever setting her own house in order. Let me read three or four statements from the Morgenthau plan, and I ask hon. members to weigh the significance of these statements. Every member has a copy of the pamphlet and, I trust, has read it with oare. I quote from Division VI:
Each member country of the Fund-
Which would be the name of the supranational government to which we would subscribe.
Each member country of the Fund undertakes the following:

I go down the list and read 3C, and I commend it to every hon. member of this house:
Such other measures as the Fund shall recommend-
Perhaps I should read No. 1 in order to show how that passage fits in:
' To maintain by appropriate action exchange rates established by the Fund on the currencies of other countries and not to alter exchange rates except w-ith the consent of the Fund and only to the extent and in the direction approved by the Fund. Exchange rates of member countries may be permitted to fluctuate within a specified range fixed by the Fund.
There is a great deal more in that than appears on the surface. And now 3C:
Such other measures as the Fund shall recommend-
In other words, if the Fund saw fit to recommend that Canada completely dismantle her beet sugar industry, Canada would do it. If the Fund saw fit to recommend that Canada should go out of the sheep business entirely, Canada would humbly do it. Let me read 5:
To give consideration to the views of the Fund on any existing or proposed monetary or economic policy the effect of which would be to bring about sooner or later serious disequilibrium in the balance of payments of other countries.
If Canada had signed an agreement like that, in vain would the hon. member for Davenport make that excellent suggestion of his with respect to using the waters of the Saskatchewan river in order to bless the whole of the dried area of central Canada, because the Fund could prevent that being done on the plea that it would upset the economy of Canada. Again, take No. 7:
To adopt appropriate legislation or decrees to carry out its undertakings to the Fund and to facilitate the activities of the Fund.
I mention this in passing to indicate the sort of thing to which Canada might blindly commit herself if she accepted the proposals of many of these planners who are having so much to say and to do in connection with the building up of the new order which is to be. Social Crediters are unalterably opposed to committing Canada to any such proposal, which would interfere with the ability of this country to put her own house in order and to govern herself.
Another principle which we advocate with respect to international relations is this: to maintain our armed forces at a strength adequate for national defence under the sovereign control of the people of Canada, and in no circumstances to surrender such control to any external authority. Far be it from us to accept the principle of any international police force, the activities of which might be 
governed by a Sir Montagu Norman or a Sir Otto Neimeyer, or a Mr. McKitrick, of Uie United States, or any junta of men meeting at Basel, Switzerland. We advocate that Canada maintain control of her own forces and keep them at a sufficient degree of efficiency .to enable her to discharge her responsibilities in the world to come.
Another principle we advocate is this: To recognize the sovereign integrity of all other nations and to exercise scrupulous care not to interfere in the internal affairs of any other country.
Again, we believe that Canada should abolish all unnecessary' barriers to trade and to travel, and that Canada should make available to the nations whose domestic needs require them, on reasonable and mutually agreeable conditions, the raw materials of which Canada has an abundance. Let me recall the importance of considering Japan in this connection. Just now, I know, our feelings towards Japan are heated, but the day will come when the world will be at peace and we must look upon Japan not as an enemy but as a friend, and look sympathetically upon the plight with which she is faced, with 77,000,000 people in the area, small and restricted as well as unproductive, in which Providence has placed her.
Further, we advocate that we strive consistently with other nations for the establishment of good-will among the peoples of the world. It is utterly impossible to establish good-will among the peoples of the world while our nation has a high standard of living and other nations are unable to procure the necessities of life; while the Japanese, for instance, are working at a low standard of living, as are the Hindus and the Indian people, and Canada a.t the high standard of living which is possible for us. It will be utterly impossible to have international goodwill under such circumstances.
May I say a word with regard to foreign trade. Our trade relations with other countries should be based upon the reciprocal and mutually agreeable exchange of surplus goods and surplus services. In bringing into being this policy we should observe certain financial principles. I will lay down these principles. We have no use for any such schemes as the two to which I have referred, which are pernicious from beginning to end and are designed to enslave mankind. On the contrary, we favour these principles: First, that there shall be a complete abandonment of the so-called gold standard or any gold basis for the control of the national economy. Gold has enslaved mankind for thousands of

Supply-External Affairs
years, and gold will always enslave mankind wherever it may be used as the basis for currency. Second, that the home market shall be provided with sufficient purchasing power to buy the goods offered for sale at economic .prices. This principle has never yet been applied in the history of the world, never once, and it has never been dreamed of in the Dominion of Canada. I doubt if the Prime Minister conceives of it to-day.

The fourth principle is that each province shall be given a voice in the allocation of the settlers within its boundaries. I am not making a pronouncement one way or another on the question I now mention, but in my province we have a problem created by the Hutterites. Assume that a Hutterite colony came in and settled near Ottawa, in the outskirts. They would continue to increase, they would buy up additional pieces of land, and in due time there would be a ring of Hutterite colonies around Ottawa. The Ontario government would be helpless to deal with the problem, because to-day this is a dominion matter. Every law that Ontario might pass to deal with the question would be disallowed by Ottawa, just as the Prime Minister took action recently to disallow a law which Alberta passed in an endeavour to deal with the Hutterite situation. What would be the result if this were allowed to go on for two hundred years? What freedom, justice and liberty would there be in the province of Ontario? It was easy for the dominion government to make an agreement with the Hutterites and then leave the provinces to take the rap. The provinces are still taking the rap, and the dominion is just doing nothing about it. The application of my fourth principle would overcome this problem. It would make the dominion a little more cautious about what kind of agreement it entered into.
The fifth principle is that a proper standard of living shall be assured the present population of Canada before allowing an influx of immigrants who have no assets or visible means of support. There will arise in the minds of many the question: what is the use of admitting more immigrants into Canada when we are unable to give employment to the people who are already here? It may be proposed that we shall admit only those who can contribute to our production, of shoes, for example-I understand that certain Czechs came in to manufacture shoes. Now another question immediately arises in the minds of every fact-facing man. What are we going to do about the shoes we are at present producing and which will be displaced by the production of those Czechs? Where are we going to sell the goods? No matter from what angle we view this question of immigration, we find cause for anxiety and concern.
May I raise four questions of criticism of the Prime Minister's efforts before I sit down? There are great problems to be solved. I began to talk about these problems last night when I discussed inflation. I know I make myself

annoying to many members of the House of Commons when I begin to discuss money matters; but I know positively as a responsible member of this House of Commons, understanding the money question, that it is my duty to discuss monetary matters before my fellow members, just as in 1936, 1937 and 1938 it was my duty to discuss the question of beet sugar in this country. I discussed beet sugar with very little respect from the Liberal side, but on that question I was right and they were wrong. It is possible that history may repeat itself this time with respect to money. Again, I shall probably be found right, my critics wrong. From time to time therefore I propose to raise these questions of the way in which to attain freedom from want and fear.
What is the use of having our prime ministers and presidents meet out on the Atlantic and plan a united nations Atlantic charter if we have no way in the world by which the charter's proposals can be implemented, if we have nothing to suggest to overcome what for many years has proved to be deficient? We simply must find a method of doing things in a new way.
I am going to point out the things which I find deficient in the Prime Minister's speech. He did not show us how to carry on trade without trade wars, which means, so far as he knows or has suggested to this country, the minute this war is over we shall begin trade wars again and be sowing the seeds of another war. Inevitably we ourselves will be contributing to the cause of the next war and will blame everybody else but ourselves, just as in this war, after we had abundantly caused the war we blamed Hitler because he started it.
Again the Prime Minister has not shown that he knows anything at all about how to increase home markets or how to increase home consumption-that is, to increase the purchasing power within Canada and to raise the standard of living of the Canadian people without incurring more debt or resorting to more taxation. If he did indicate any such knowledge in any of the speeches that lie has delivered since the outbreak of the war, I shall be very thankful to have someone point out the time and place so that I may refer to it.
The Prime Minister did not tell how to build up international cooperation without such loss of sovereignty as will impair Canada's ability to manage her own household. May I repeat that if the new order which is to be established, if the new international cooperation, involves anything like the international currency stabilization proposal, then it will destroy all possibility of achieving the object for which it is designed. It is supposed to

Supply-External Affairs
increase the prosperity of the world; it will decrease the prosperity of the world and render world conditions utterly hopeless. The Prime Minister has not shown how any such evil result can be avoided. He speaks of international cooperation. Finally the Prime Minister has not shown how to maintain adequate fighting forces-probably this is a bit premature-in Canada and in the British empire to put the empire and this country on a permanent basis of security.
Surely every hon. member of this committee must find his heart filled with misgiving when he looks back into the past and remembers that in 1920 and 1921 the British empire was unchallengeably supreme, and when he reflects that if the British peoples had maintained their military strength to a standard comparable with that maintained in 1920 and 1921 there never could have been a Hitler world without end, and there never could have been any attack on Ethiopia world without end. Yet what happened in the Dominion of Canada? What happened in Britain? The superb navy was in large measure dismantled; the splendid fighting forces were allowed to fall into disuse. What happened in Canada? I hope I shall not offend the Progressive Conservatives over much when I recall to them that it was under the administration of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett that the nails were driven into the coffin of the fighting forces of Canada. What was the reason? We could not afford it; we could not afford to maintain soldiers and airmen. In the light of what has happened since, what ridiculous nonsense!
If the Progressive Conservatives were to gain power after this war, have they indicated by any remarks they have made that they would know any better than to do that same foolhardy thing over again? Have they, by one single word? Has the Prime Minister indicated that he knows how the enormous sums of money can be raised with which to maintain a fighting force comparable to that in which we rejoice at the present time, and which soon will make us supreme in the military affairs of the world? It ought to be possible to maintain a fighting force which will render us secure. I do not wish to disagree unduly with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, but I should like to point out-

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this discussion I do not do so with any desire to

place added criticism on the shoulders of the man who is carrying what has been truly called' the awful burden of attending to the affairs of Canada in this crisis; 'but it is usually the custom to take advantage of this item to discuss the relationship of Canada with foreign nations, and I wish to exercise that privilege now.
British Columbia is waiting very anxiously for the words that may fall from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to-day, waiting for a lead, waiting for a declaration of policy on a matter about which they are exceedingly bitter. I have lived there for forty-seven years and I have never seen British Columbia so strongly united on one subject and at the same time so bitter about it; "therefore I think this is a proper time to ask the Prime Minister what his policy will be, first as regards the Japanese who are now in Canada and second, those who are now in Japan. We had a discussion a few days ago about it, therefore I need not rehash what was said then. However, I am going to take up a little time to explain the case at least to eastern members who are not so well informed and who have come into the house only comparatively recently.
Away back some fifty years ago, when oriental immigration first began, British Columbia became annoyed about the class and numbers of immigrants that were coming from China at that time. They were of a coolie type, and they were dangerous to our economic well-being. Pressure was brought to bear on the government and they put a tax of $50 on every Chinaman who came into the country. Well, that did not do any good, and they raised it to $100 and later on to $500, and still it was ineffective for this reason. The Chinaman mortgaged his soul and everything else he possessed to some Chinese financial company which put up the $500, and the wretched immigrant was simply a peon to that company for many years, until he had paid it back. The Japanese were dealt with by some form of gentleman's agreement. We have had several versions of it which usually worked well for a little while, until the wily oriental discovered a way of evading them.
I shall now deal with the Chinese. Along about 1923 the government passed legislation excluding entirely all Chinese immigrants, or practically all. Of course members of 'the diplomatic corps, and a few persons of that type, were allowed in. But to all intents and purposes the Chinese-the labouring class and every other class-were prohibited from settling in this country. It has worked. I pressed the government very much at that
Supply-External Affairs

time-I begged 'them-to apply the same treatment to all orientals, to use the word "orientals" rather than "Chinese". However the government did not do it. Along about 1928 or 1929 the government amended the gentleman's agreement, so far as the Japanese were concerned, to make it more effective. And yet sooner or later the Japanese found a way of shooting holes in it.
I never let uip in my efforts, and along about 1938, after I had been watching all the time, trying to .press this thing, because I knew how deeply it concerned the people of my province, and eighteen months before the war, I thought I saw a chance when conditions were more favourable, and as a result I brought in bill No. 11, which placed the Japanese in exactly the same position as the Chinese are. In that bill I simply used the word "oriental" instead of the word "Chinese". This was exactly the same type of bill that had been passed fifteen years earlier in regard to -the Chinese. The government voted it down, saying that it would be displeasing to the Japanese, and that .they did not wish to have any possibility of trouble with the imperial government.
I then introduced bill No. 38, which was entirely different. It provided an educational test, and was designed to keep out orientals. It followed largely the form of the measure recommended by the Eight Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, about which the hon. member for Vancouver South spoke the other day. Mr. Chamberlain strongly urged Canada to adopt the Natal act. It was almost word for word with that act, an act which has kept the orientals out of New Zealand and Australia, and I believe South Africa, for thirty years. The government opposed it on a technicality and the bill was thrown out. Later however I had a chance to reintroduce it. It then became bill No. 112, with the technicality taken care of. This second bill forbade the immigration of anyone-it did not refer to Japanese, Chinese or any others specifically-who could not pass a reading test in the French, English or some language or dialect to be found in Europe. This excluded about seventy-five per cent of the world's population, so that it could not be said that it was aimed at excluding only Japanese. And it would have had the effect of carrying out all the principles of the Natal act. This was opposed by the government.
Alt this point I should like to quote a few remarks I made on that occasion. The government had declared their intention of defeating this bill also, but without giving any reasons against it-because the reasons
I Mr WeHl.1
alleged against the earlier bill were nonexistent so far as this one was concerned. It was not directed against Chinese or Japanese particularly, but affected about seventy-five per cent of the world's population. This is what I said as reported at page 3410 of Hansard, 11938:
Is it because the government get political hysterics every time the name of Japan is mentioned? We dare not deal with the strictly domestic matter of our own immigration for fear-and fear is an ugly word, Mr. Speaker- that an alien heathen nation, that has no claim whatever to a grievance, might not like it, a nation whose best claim to fame at the present moment is the fact that it is raping and ravaging a friendly nation whose territory it swore a few short years ago to protect and maintain.	.
Now, this thing is cumulative. Where is it going to stop? If we yield five per cent of our rights to-day for the sake of peace, six months hence we shall be required to surrender ten per cent, and a year afterwards they will want fifty per cent. Other nations will imitate this policy, and we shall lose their respect.
How did we get their respect? We became a nation, not by the Statute of Westminster alone that we hear so much about, but through the blood and treasure we spent in France to prevent Canada from becoming a German colony. The Statute of Westminster did something. It gave us power to make our own treaties. A lot of good that did us. If we set our feet on the fatal, bitter path I have outlined, soon we shall not be allowed to make our own treaties; we shall not even be allowed to make our own pyjamas, because Japan will discover that she can make them cheaper because of her low standard of living, and sell them cheaper in Toronto than the cost of the raw material. If that is to be our policy, we had better tear up the Statute of Westminster and crawl back as a colony under the overburdened protection of the British nation. At least we would be safe there; yes, cheaply safe, would we not? Britain would give it to us, give it to us to the last exhaustion of her strained powers, and she would not worry and fuss because every now and again we debate whether we would be at war when she is at war. But what a humiliation it would be f-or- us as a nation and as individuals! . . .
And further on I said this:
To-night we are at the forks of the road. We can say to Japan: "We have not passed this bill because we thought you might not like it. We have not exactly cut loose from Britain, but we have indicated that there is no obligation, that there are no commitments if she is in trouble and to that extent we have weakened her in the eyes of the world; you have our sympathy; we hope you will not be too hard on us." Shall we take that degrading and humiliating position, or shall we say to Japan and to the world, "When Britain is in trouble we are in trouble; when Britain is at war we are at war, and when Britain is at war while we cannot bind future parliaments as to the amount of participation, any more than the British parliament is bound, we will do our part; we are solidly behind Great Britain economically, financially and in every other way to the best of our ability." Then, let us say to Japan, "We are determined to run and

Supply-External Affairs
control our own domestic affairs, of which immigration is one, and another is to decide whether people can be deported or not. That is another privilege and we are going to use it. We are solidly behind the British nation, and the British nation is solidly behind us." That would be the end of it. That would be a policy of courage, a policy of dignity and self-respect, both for us and from the other nations, and one that would make for the preservation of peace, a bold policy which would put us in standing and reputation with all the nations of the world. Whether we take the short vision of the immediate future or the long vision down the vista of time, it would be a policy that would immediately and ultimately work for the benefit of British Columbia, of Canada and of the British empire in which we are all concerned. I think the first step towards the announcement and the initiation of such a policy would be for us to pass this bill which is before us to-night.
Remember, that was eighteen months before the war. How prophetically true some of it is to-day. It was opposed by the government, and defeated by a somewhat smaller majority -much smaller-than usual.
I pause here to wonder. I wonder if when the Japanese government decided to go to war they were at all influenced by what took place that night in the House of Commons in 1938. No sane person in Canada, no Canadian, doubted that we would line up as we have lined up. But the oriental mind is not the occidental mind. When they read these repeated utterances with respect to our making no commitments, when they realized how quickly and urgently we had acted at the time of the last war but were now making no commitments, and actually voting down the bill I have mentioned-one which did not apply directly to the Japanese, but applied to seventy-five per cent of the world's population-they, in their oriental minds might have thought-and, of course, wrongly-that we as a nation were unwilling to displease the Japanese, and that we might possibly stay neutral, or have a neutral attitude in the event of a war. A firm stand then on our part would at least not have been open to any misconception in the oriental mind.
But, be that as it may, my thought in speaking now is to urge that we face the situation as it is. W'hat we want now-and I know I speak for the people of British Columbia-is to know whether the government is now prepared to pass a bill for the exclusion of the Japanese-to prevent any further immigration. Is the government also *prepared to insist at the peace conference that the Japanese in Canada will be repatriated? I would ask the Prime Minister, if he favours us with a reply, not to pass this issue off by saying, "Our first business is to win the war; it will be time enough to discuss
other matters afterwards." No, it will be too late then, because repatriation will have to be one of the terms of peace, because, once peace is declared, a British subject could not be deported. But it can be done through the terms of peace. We are only asking for an announcement of the policy of the Prime Minister and his government in days to come-we are not asking him to do something which would embarrass him in his relations with other nations at the moment, but that he will prohibit the Japanese from entering Canada hereafter. We ask also for an assurance that at the peace conference-we know he cannot do everything he likes, but we do know the great influence he must possess there on account of the part that Canada has played in this war-he will use that great influence in favour of repatriation of the Japs. So the two things we ask now are that he gives us the assurance that he will prohibit Japanese immigration into Canada for all time, and use his influence at the peace conference for the repatriation of all persons of Japanese origin.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to interrupt the committee's proceedings but I rise to a question of privilege. I have deferred bringing it up before because I wanted to get some dates that I have now received, and regarding which I should like to make a statement.
I refer hon. members to the statement made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury last night as it appears in Hansard at page 4533. After the Minister of Labour had spoken the hon. member said:
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury):	I have only
to observe that that was not the case with respect to the government's man-power policy in the early stages.
The Minister of Labour had said that if any statement of policy were to be made he would make it in the house. Then the hon. member for York-Sunbury goes on:
Who laid down the policy for the Department of National Defence after the mobilization act was passed? Who was the government's spokesman before the Canadian club at Ottawa but the chief of general staff of this country when the minister did not have the guts to get up and do it himself.
The hon. member refers to the policy with regard to the thirty-day training programme which was put into force in 1940, and the implication, and not only the implication but the statement is there, that the minister had not the courage to make an announcement in the house with regard to that policy but left it to the chief of the general staff to make the announcement. I have looked up the facts
Supply-External Affairs

and the dates, and if the hon. member had been sticking to the facts he would have said that, on July 29, 1940, three months before the chief of the general staff spoke on the subject, I made a very full statement in the house with regard to the government's defence programme in which I dealt particularly with the thirty-day training policy. I do not propose to trouble the committee by reading that statement of mine with regard to the thirty-day training plan. It appears in Hansard of July 29, 1940, at pages 2094 and 2096.
In order to ascertain whether there could have been any doubt in the public mind about the minister having made such a statement I looked at the newspapers and I found that the Montreal Gazette of July 30, 1940, nearly three months before the chief of the general staff spoke to the Canadian club, carried this headline right across the front page:
Drafted militia to start training October 1 [DOT]-Will call 30,000 monthly for thirty days of army drill under new defence policy.
On the same page of the Gazette appears a summary by the Canadian Press in which this paragraph [DOT] appears:
Compulsory training of men called starts October 1 with 30,000 a month called and trained thereafter.
I might add that on September 13, 1940, over a month before the chief of the general staff made his speech to the Canadian club, the proclamation with respect to the thirty-days training was issued and appeared in the papers of this country on September 19, 1940. Further, in order that it may be understood that the public was thoroughly acquainted with the thirty-days training policy which I as the minister principally concerned had announced in the house on July 29, the first camp was held on October 9, 1940, two weeks before the chief of the general staff made his speech to the Canadian club.
With these facts before him, Mr. Chairman, one can hardly understand a member of this house, and particularly a member of the legal profession, who ought to be careful in regard to the facts when making a statement, making the statement which the hon. member for York-Sunbury did last night, indicating that the chief of the general staff had to make this announcement on behalf of the minister because the minister did not have the guts to make the announcement himself.
I want to add that General Crerar was not the spokesman for the government. This matter has been brought up twice before by my hon. friend and on the last occasion he had the propriety to withdraw the statement which he had made to the effect that the chief of the general staff was put up by the

government to introduce the subject of thirty-days training. The hon. member withdrew that statement and his withdrawal appears at page 1556 of Hansard of March 14, 1941.
All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is that on both counts my hon. friend's statement is incorrect and without any foundation whatever. I do not want to lengthen the discussion or add to the acidity of the remarks my hon. friend has made, but I do want to say that at least in my humble opinion my hon. friend is entirely too prone to make on the spur of the moment interjections which are not in line with facts. I want to say further that we might expect better of my hon. friend in that respect as a member of my own profession. To make a statement regarding a member which is wholly unfounded in fact is bad enough, but to make it in the language which my hon. friend used, which was both crude and offensive, is an offence against the rules of debate, and I ask my hon. friend to withdraw the statement in its entirety. I leave it to him to make any amends he thinks are appropriate under the circumstances, having regard to the relations that exist between members of this house.

speechtext:
I wish to say just a few words in this debate. The Prime Minister need not weary in well doing, and he may take comfort in the reflection that there has never been a subject like foreign affairs on which any two persons in this country have agreed. There will always be wide differences of opinion between those who do not and those who do take the view that the British empire has been, throughout the ages, the agency that has promoted the welfare of humanity and preserved the liberties of civilization. We have two great races in this country who were allies in the last war, and our partners of that time deserved a better fate than befell them.
I suggest that we have never had a foreign policy in Canada. This debate has shown the wavering and the doubts and fears which many members have had in this house. It seems that some hon. members have always wanted to depend on other people for our security-on peace pacts, on- leagues, on doctrines of collective security, on pan-Americanism, the Monroe doctrine, the Kellogg pact, the Locarno treaty, the Briand pact and many other promises of that sort. These gentlemen have always depended upon these props for the security of this country.
Now is the time for us to recapture the spirit of the empire, because if we do not recapture that spirit when the country is at war we shall forget all about it when the war is over. There has been the same trouble in all the democratic countries, Canada, the mother country and the United States. Not one of these ever had a foreign policy. Canada has never had a foreign policy, nor has the United States, and the result is that we found ourselves in this awful war. When the great Napoleonic war which lasted for twenty-three years, from 1793 on, broke out, it found Britain unprepared. We nearly lost that war, the first half of which ended in the peace of Amiens in 1801. The British people at that time were depending on the hope of peace and on the pacifist spirit and had no adequate forces for defence, and the war that broke out again in 1801, and lasted until 1815 again saw the British people unprepared, although they won it. Again, the twenty years between these two great modern wars, 1918 to 1938, have been the most disastrous in
the history of civilization. In fact, civilization was nearly ended when in 1939 this present war broke out.
If we are to continue this state of affairs we are going to have another war and it will not be very long after this one is over. I say to the Prime Minister: Do not forget, in dealing with foreign affairs, that Russia is not at war with Japan, nor is China at war with Germany. Do not forget these two principles. We are allied to two great imperial powers, splendid countries, the United States and Russia. They may not be imperial in the sense of wanting to grab territory; that remains to be seen. But if we are to judge by certain things that have been said in the United States senate and congress with reference to this question, we cannot be too sure on this point. One senator, from Maryland, wishes to have outright possession of the British Caribbean bases. Senator Reynolds of North Carolina wants Wrangel island and certain Dutch possessions in the western hemisphere to go to the United States, and other senators want Bermuda and so on. They also make reference to the lease-lend act. I say, they may not be imperial in the sense of wanting to appropriate territory,, but some of their leading public men have indicated a desire for something of that sort.
Russia is in the same position. They are imperial like the United States in the sense that they want to have a much larger share in world affairs and a much larger share in the peace terms and in the new world to come, and unless Canada is wrapped up with the British empire, unless she is part and parcel of the commonwealth to which we belong, her position may be precarious, and we shall have little say in the peace terms. The Canadian people have shown unequivocally that they want to remain in the empire. The old empire may have gone but there is a new empire to take its place, and it will stand, as the old empire has always stood down through the ages, for all that will advance the cause of humanity. The people of this country, on the occasion of the visit of their majesties in 1939, showed the tremendous popularity of the monarchy in Canada. That spirit was demonstrated in all our provinces and nowhere more fully than in Quebec where the school children gave them such a magnificent reception.
I believe in a foreign policy for Canada. We have none at the present time. Can any hon. member tell me what the foreign policy of Canada was before the war? We had none. We had no foreign policy in the twenty years that intervened between the first great war
Supply-External Affairs

and this one. As I say, there were people in this country who were depending upon pacifist agencies that preached international security and international peace, for the preservation of the freedom which we, in common with the people in the rest of the empire, have enjoyed for so long. But all these peace hopes collapsed in 1939 and we found ourselves in this greatest war of all times.
Let us not forget the lessons of history in this regard. One eminent author has made this statement. He says that we are gambling with the lives and happiness of millions, and the human race is in jeopardy. We cannot be forever blowing bubbles and talking a lot of salon sentimental nonsense about the true Germans. If that is what a voluble selfrighteous section of the British intelligentsia have been talking for the past twenty years, he says, then it is hopeless.
In the twenty years between the two wars the democracies all lost the sense of self-preservation in their lunatic policies of disarmament. They no longer thought it necessary that we should have armies, navies or air forces. They simply abandoned any attempt at self-preservation, and that apathy helped to bring on this war. Political apathy and ignorance are the axis' best friends. The same propaganda is going on now, and we are faced with a total lack of any foreign policy. This is equally true of the United States and the mother country. No great country has ever existed for so long a time with so little in the form of a foreign policy as the United States. A foreign policy involves certain commitments in the way of preparedness, but the United States, Britain, and Canada as well, thought of nothing but disarmament. As I say, we had lost the instinct of self-preservation. The fact is that we have never really studied the German political soul in all its horror. As Mrs. Maxse in England has said: We are fighting against a deadweight of dead yesterdays, and Germany has been strong because we have been the ally of laissez-faire. We have fought two world wars in the space of one generation because we would not face the facts. Germany has fought five great wars in the last eighty years and there will be another war. But people will be found who will talk about poor old Germany and allow her to rebuild after this second great conflict. The German people are the same yesterday, to-day and forever. The first I learned about them was in reading Tacitus and the story of the Holy Roman Empire by Bryce and Gibbon, and then we come to the wars	of Frederick the Great, at
Silesia, and continue on to the last war and this one. Yes, Mr. Chairman; the German people are the same yesterday, to-day and forever, and there is no use slobbering over these people. They hate Britain, they hate Canada, they hate the British empire. They are out to beat the rest of the world because they want wmrld domination. If we allow this thing to happen there will be a third war. That is what may happen if we accept the position that has been proposed in this house in the last few days as the basis of our foreign policy. Are we to depend upon some other international body? There will always be nations. Are we to depend upon a new pacifist league or some such thing, as was said in the house on July 1? I am absolutely opposed to this doctrine and I have been consistently opposed to it. You will have to arm all along the line and keep armed. After this war is over you will find that our great allies to the south will be isolationists again. I read the debates of the Senate and the House of Representatives and I know what is happening. That country speaks with two voices. Those people are our friends and neighbours, we are fond of them, we have good relations with them because they are our kith and kin, but after all is said and done they will respect us much more if we tell them the truth, if we tell them what we are doing to preserve peace and progress in the world. I know a great many United States people and I have a great many friends in that country. I believe the average United States citizen would be better pleased if the people of this country stood up for their own country once in a while.
We have a glorious empire and the administration of our colonial empire will be one of the glorious pages of history. I believe in what Mr. Churchill said the other day. and I think the overwhelming majority of this country do so as well. He said that he had not become Prime Minister in order to see the empire liquidated, or to see the empire go down under the hammer by default. If she does go down, what will happen to Canada? Canada needs the empire and the empire needs Canada. Great Britain needs the United States just as much as the United States needs Great Britain. I believe in what Mr. Churchill said. I know that our new empire to come after this war will do its duty towards civilization and liberty as it has always done in the past.
We are a democracy, and every democracy that I know of that has existed between the two wars has depended upon the pacifist agencies I have named. We will have the same trouble again. Now is the time to change

Supply-External Affairs
and adopt a different policy. We were not alone in following this course. Other democracy countries became helpless. They thought that everything was over, that there would be no war, that they could disarm and depend upon the league and notes. I have sat in this house for years and I have read the debates that took place in the twenty years between the two wars. I know the attitude adopted by the isolationists and separatists; they contended that we could depend upon these agencies. I can remember March 31, 1939, when a bill was introduced by the former member for Selkirk, Hon. Mr. Thorson. When that bill was proposed if war came Canada should be a neutral country. It sought to define the status of Canada as a belligerent. At that time we had nothing to be belligerent with because we had thrown everything away. There was some support for this bill from all sides of the house, but I opposed it. I have been charged with the unforgivable sin of having been proved to Be right all along on the armament question between the two wars. I was in advance of public opinion om many of these matters, and right along I was in favour of full cooperation and coordination with Great Britain.
I am absolutely opposed to any policy that will bring us into any pan-<American union. We are friends in trade and for peace with them as always. That would be fatal to this country. We have no right to make some political or military agreement with the Latin powers or any other country which have been named in this agreement. Do not forget that these Latin republics are under the lend-lease act. When the lend-lease act was first conceived the United States wras neutral. They had the Johnson act which outlined the status of a belligerent, and treated the axis the same as the peace nations, and they had a cash-and-carry policy, up to six months before the days of Pearl Harbor. Then the lease-lead act came into being but Germany had been given an opportunity to develop her submarine warfare, as the Neutrality Act presented Germany with an Atlantic fleet. This act was devised to enable the countries fighting the axis to obtain United States arms. Then Pearl Harbor happened and we declared war the day after. The Prime Minister acted promptly in the matter.
We nearly had a Pearl Harbor ourselves in the St. Lawrence at St. Pierre-Miquelon. This was prevented by General de Gaulle going in there at the request of the inhabitants and taking over the islands in order to prevent them from falling into German hands. The people on these islands have been friends of Britain for many years
past. When congress declared war the United States declared to bring the conflict to a successful determination and they pledged all the resources of the country to that end. The agreement which the Latin countries who are recipients of the lend-lease have signed contains a clause providing for free commercial intercourse after the war and the reduction of tariffs and all trade barriers. I do not think we should enter a pan-American agreement under circumstances like that. If you do you are going to have another league of nations made up of these countries, some of which have been friendly to our enemies. I am absolutely opposed to that. We have no right to enter into such an arrangement over the heads of other members of the empire. What we want is a united empire and a united policy, not only during the course of the war but when the war is over.
Great Britain should not be blamed for all the things that have been done on foreign policy, because some of the things done in the name of Britain were asked for by the dominions. Look at the statute of Westminster, for instance. I always opposed that in this house. It was in that statute that we heard the high-sounding words "commonwealth of nations". I think I heard them for the first time, used by Lord Rosebery in 1905. In my opinion this is" simply an empire-wrecking statute that divided the dominion and empire, and it is one of the reasons why we have had a second war. I do not know whether Australia or New Zealand have signed it yet, but I believe it has been up recently for discussion. We shall have to have a foreign policy based on the principle that right plus might is right. No longer can -we throw away our defence. We shall have, to be armed. You will find after the war certain people will again become isolationists and therefore our foreign policy with the rest of the empire should be right plus might is right. Whether or not we shall have that remains to be seen. I hope we shall not help these people to go up to Geneva near Orillia. They should take a holiday this year. I do not know v7hy a fine county like Sirncoe has to have these pacifists, isolationists and others. They are the most motley pacifist collection of people I have ever seen. All they do there is talk international pacifism and if they have their w'ay we will have another war. Some of them are all right, but most of them were-wrong during the pre-war days and have been wrong on foreign policy for twenty-two years.
I believe it is only fair to say that this country in the twenty years between the two wars was the chief drifter from empire policy
Supply-External Affairs

In the imperial conference of 1937 when these matters came up we said we had no commitments; parliament would decide. We were asked about a shipping policy, an empire shipping policy. The Prime Minister will correct me if I am wrong, as I have not the book with me, but it was said we had no commitments, that parliament would decide. I do not quarrel with that although I personally object to that policy. There was nothing new about it. Other countries were doing the same as to disarmament as Canada. It was felt there would be no more wars, therefore it was not necessary to have any more navies, armies or air force. What happened? We threw away our defences as well as our friends and did not see a new war coming.
I was glad to read the remarks made by Mr. Churchill the other day in connection with foreign affairs. History will show that Mr. Chamberlain was one of England's greatest men. The same applies to the whole Chamberlain family. A Munich was necessary because neither Britain nor France singly or collectively were ready for war and were no match for Germany. We heard statements in room 16 the other day about the utter lack of any defences or preparations of the mother country. Had it not been for Munich and the one year's respite, the empire would have gone, Britain would have lost the war and Hitler would have been in London in no time. Therefore we should pay tribute to the mother country for what it has done to save us in this country after Dunkirk, and also what it has done in connection with protection on the Atlantic and on the Pacific.
The keystone of the policy should be that no British territory shall be handed over to any international control. The United States will not give away any territory. They will not give away Alaska, the Panama canal or any other part of their territory. Some people want Bermuda to be taken away from the empire. Others want Russia to hand over Wrangel island. As part of the British empire our policy should be to back up Great Britain and the other dominions to the extent that the empire shall not be liquidated. Are we going to support a policy of throwing away the people in the colonies of the empire, people who have stood by the empire in its darkest days, because some other power wants to grab them?
I believe the people of this country are overwhelmingly behind the people of the mother country. They are anxious to see the right thing done at the peace conference so that the empire does not go by default.
In view of the commitments which are proposed I am pleased to see that Canada has so
[Mr Church.]
far kept out of lease-lend entanglements because of the grave dangers that lie ahead after the war. Owing to disarmament the empire has had to give bases fsorn Newfoundland to British Guiana to the United States in return for some fifty-six old destroyers, many of which were obsolete. Many of them have had to return to Annapolis for repairs. It was a most unfortunate .position for the people of the countries concerned and the dominions to be placed in. For the last one hundred years certain people have wanted the territory to which I have referred. Because of the lease-lend provisions it will be difficult at the peace conference to settle these empire matters. These bases have been leased for ninety-nine years, which is practically freehold.
Last Sunday there was held in Toronto a glorious fourth of July service at St. Paul's Anglican church, Toronto. The Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition were invited to be present, but unfortunately they could not be there. At that service a stone was presented to St. Paul's, Toronto, by the Bishop of Maryland. Speaking of our relations with the United States, Bishop Renison said:
There is an unwritten bond between the peoples of the United States of America and those who live in the far-flung British empire. It is not true that the British, or even the English, are of one blood. Their various flexible types, ideas and originality bear witness to the mingling, through their long history, of the Anglo-Saxons, the Celts, the Romans and the Normans. The same thing is more apparently true concerning Americans. Some one asked whether there was a special prayer for Americans in the old English Prayer Book and the answer was: "You can find it in the petition for all sorts and conditions of men." But a wise Englishman happily replied: "That petition was made for the English and it fits them."
Speaking generally, we have the same history; we come from the same stock; we have the same heroes between the 10th and 18th centuries. Long before there was any thought of a formal alliance of the English-speaking peoples, there was a mystic tie which united them in spite of themselves and without their knowledge.
We are all influenced by our history. In that glorious eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews you can find the honour roll of the people of Israel. It comes as a surprise to us to learn that the old prophets did not hesitate to speak to their people of the glorious deeds of their ancestors with a religious intensity. We too easily take it for granted that we must look to the Sacred Canon alone for our inspiration and comfort in these days of world destiny. If we could reincarnate the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, he would ask us to turn our eyes to the glorious history of God's dealing for a thousand years. We can image the writer making such verses as these:
By faith. Alfred the Great gathered the scattered tribes of Albion in the nine century, and laid the foundation of the English nation.

By faith, Edward the Confessor builded Westminster Abbey, to be a shrine forever in lands not yet discovered.
By faith, John Wycliffe translated the Word of God from a dead language into a living tongue.
By faith, Drake and Raleigh sailed the uncharted seas and carried the soul of England to distant parts of the world.
By faith, John Milton w'rote of Paradise Lost, and, when he was blind, sang of the city where they need no candle, neither light of the sun.
By faith, John Hampden resisted a tyrant king and died for liberty on Chalgrove Field.
By faith, Abraham Lincoln freed the slaves and saved the Union; hopeful in disaster, in victory he was merciful, and with charity toward all and hatred toward none he strove to bind up his nation's wounds. In dying, he joined the Immortals.
By faith, Thomas Edison searched for the ifts which God had hidden for men to find; e made the deaf to hear; he made his country a family; and to those who since the beginning of life on this planet had nightly sat in darkness he turned their night into day.
He then speaks of Shakespeare, and continues ;
In Lincoln in Chicago there is a statute to the greatest man that England ever produced. He was not a soldier, but a poet. Here is the inscription:
"He was not for an age, but for all time, our many-minded Shakespeare." . . .
The Niagara river is a parable of the story of the English-speaking people. It is the dividing line between the British empire and America. The waters coming from the great inland seas are compressed into the swift rapids of the Niagara river-a symbol of the early difficulties and misunderstandings of the 18th century. Then we come to the great cataract, which stands for the revolution and the separate destiny of the two English-speaking nations. Below there is the whirlpool and the gorge of the 19th century, with alternate rapids and still water succeeding each other; and then the river emerges into lake Ontario, and beyond that it flows through the great river of _ the St. Lawrence, ever wider and deeper, until it reaches the ocean.
Such is the story of our people.
The last war produced some great soldiers who have had a lot to do with the destiny of this country. I was at a service the Sunday before last for the Canadian corps and the Canadian legion in Riverdale park in my constituency, and all soldiers of the Toronto district. A great sermon was preached by the chaplain of the Queen's Own regiment. It was preached by a friend of the present Prime Minister, a friend of the Leader of the Opposition, and of the other leaders in the house. I refer to Lieutenant-Colonel the Right Reverend Canon H. F. D. Woodcock, canon of the Church of England, rector of Christ Church, Toronto. He spoke as a patriot about our empire, and asked that he might not be considered narrow or selfish if he were to
speak about the empire's cause rather than the united nations' cause. The Globe and Mail newspaper article states:
He pointed out that the empire's cause is humanity's cause.
"We are gratified that we have such powerful allies" he said, and expressed the hope that the ties with the allies, the United States, China, Russia, might grow even stronger. And while some might ask, "Where would we be to-day without our allies?" He reminded his audience that after all it was the motherland who had "taken the deadly thrust in her heart, but did not die."
"I make a plea" he said, "for the strengthening of the imperial ties, because I believe no separate existence, however splendid, can compare with that which we now enjoy as joint heirs with the people of the motherland, of all the glorious traditions of her past, and joint partakers with them of the world prestige and power which that present partnership affords.
"Nationalism is not going to be abolished by this war" the speaker declared. "It is as natural to mankind as family life. But nationalism must not be exclusive. You cannot reconcile universal industrialization and exclusive nationalism."
And that is right. Let me say those who are planning for the world should take notice of those words. But let us not forget that the United States and Russia entered this war because they were attacked. Great Britain, the mother country, did not enter the war because she was attacked. She entered it because of the pledge she had made to Poland. She will be known as the good Samaritan of the nations. And she bore the brunt of the war for two years, and bore it alone.
Before the closing of the session some resolution ought to be passed, voicing our thanks to our troops. In the British House of Lords a similar resolution was passed on May 19, in the name of Viscount Cranborne. These were his words:
It will, His Majesty's government have felt, be the desire of parliament to record by a formal resolution its thanks to those who have contributed to this noble success. This is not the first occasion when parliament has voted a resolution of thanks to His Majesty's fighting forces. There are other famous precedents; after the battle of the Nile, after the battle of Trafalgar, after the battle of Waterloo, after the Indian Mutiny. Those are glorious names in our history. They will be remembered so long as Britain remains a nation. They will be passed down from father to son, long after we are dead, buried or forgotten. And so I believe will it be with this battle. This great struggle in which we are engaged is not yet over. Germany, Italy and Japan are not yet beaten. The road that we have yet to travel may be long and stony. But whatever trials and sacrifices lie before us we are, I hope and believe, through the mists of war beginning to see the end, and when Hitler and Hitlerism is an evil memory of the past, the tale of this great victory that

has Been won in Africa by free men for the cause of freedom will be handed down as an example and an inspiration to our children and our children's children.
I believe the time has arrived when the Prime Minister, who has a very wide knowledge of foreign affairs, and is a more or less learned man in connection with this work, should prepare a white paper with respect to our relations with that glorious country, France. That is the country with which we were allied in the first great war. That is the country with which we fought side by side in that war. I should like to see prepared a white paper which would clarify the situation as to North Africa, and in fact clarify our whole foreign affairs position. I do not believe in referring these matters to a committee on industrial and international relations. I believe it would be better if we had a plan under which we could ask questions every few days, when the orders of the day are called. That would surely be better, because we would discuss matters as they develop, and avoid long debates of this kind.
I believe the time has come when the people of Canada should be taken more into the confidence of the government. I pleaded for this on March 21, 1939, before the war broke out, upon which occasion I called the attention of the house to what Mr. Chamberlain had said. He pointed o.ut that .the people should be given the truth and the facts. I say they should ,be given .the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth with respect to what is going on>
in connection with our foreign policy and this war, and they should be told what happened in the period of years between the two great wans. They should be given all that information. I do not believe we would have had a second world war if the people of the mother country and in allied countries had known the truth, the true state of affairs in respect of Germany, if they had known the truth about rearmament, and all that kind of thing.
On March 21, 1939 I' urged that the people should be given the facts, because if they were not allowed to have the truth we would be embarking on a course fraught with great danger. I say the time has come when we should have before us a white paper setting out the details of what has happened in North Africa, in connection with General Giraud and General de Gaulle, and all that kind of thing. There has been a great deal of criticism of this in the British House of Commons, and outside that House of Commons in the British press and also in Canada to the real facts about France. I refer particularly to the Yorkshire Post, the Manchester
IMr. Church.]
Guardian and many other newspapers over there. The people of Canada have the right to have this information. I believe it would be a good thing if the Prime Minister would consider [preparing a white paper along these lines.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temiscoua-ta): Mr. Chairman, in the first place I wish to reassure the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) that what I have to say will heLp him spend a quiet and restful weekend. I do not think the statute of Westminster means much,. I have it in my hand. It is divided into two parts, in the same fashion as any other piece of legislation. The first part is the preamble, and the second is the enacting portion, or the part that has the force of law.
The preamble contains some instructions which may refer to some understandings or agreements between the governments of the dominions, and the government of the United Kingdom, but it does not change in any way the status of the dominion. Let us consider them one after the other. The first paragraph of the preamble makes reference to past imperial conferences of 1928 and 1930. Then the second paragraph of the preamble contains these words:
The crown is the symbol of the free association of the members of the British commonwealth of nations.
This has not been enacted anywhere else than in our own constitution. It is a consideration which is true. I admit that the crown is binding all the dominions together. Then it goes on to say:
As they are united by a common allegiance to the crown, it would be in accord with the established constitutional position of all the members of the commonwealth in relation to one another that any alteration in the law touching the succession to the throne or the royal style and titles shall hereafter require the assent as well of the parliaments of all the dominions as of the parliament of the United Kingdom.
That is true. But we passed some legislation regarding the succession to the throne, and it was copied from the British act. It was a copy of what was passed at Westminster.
A great fuss was made to the effect that since the statute of Westminster His Excellency the Governor General is the direct representative of His Majesty the King. Before that he also represented the British government. We have heard some champions of autonomy declare in this country respecting the victory we have won, that His Excellency the Governor General represents only the King. What happened afterwards was that a British high com-

Supply-External Affairs
missioner was appointed in Canada, representing the British government. What difference is there between the governor general representing both the king and the British government, as obtained before, and the present condition where the governor general represents only the king and the British high commissioner represents the British government?
I should like to summarize later on a few of the provisions that are contained in the enacting part of the statute. Paragraph four of the preamble says:
And whereas it is necessary for the ratifying, confirming and establishing of certain of the said declarations and resolutions of the said Conferences that a law be made and enacted in due form by authority of the Parliament of the United Kingdom.
That is very important. I will repeat it:
And whereas it is necessary for the ratifying, confirming and establishing of certain of the said declarations and resolutions of the said Conferences that a law' 'be made and enacted in due form by authority of the Parliament of the United Kingdom.
That is true; I admit it, and that is why I contend that what is mentioned in the preamble is part of this statute, but not of the enacting part of the statute. The preamble goes on:
And whereas the Dominion of Canada, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Dominion of New Zealand, the Union of South Africa, the Irish Free State and Newfoundland have severally requested-
It was asked for by the dominions.
-and consented to the submission of a measure to the parliament of the United Kingdom for making such provision with regard to the matters aforesaid as is hereafter in this act contained;
That is, matters such as I have mentioned. But it is not what I have already mentioned which counts in the statute of Westminster, although it does refer to some understanding between the various governments. What does count is what has been decided by the House of Commons and by the House of Lords at Westminster with the approval of his majesty. The preamble concludes:
Now, therefore, be it enacted by the King's most Excellent Majesty by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by authority of the same, as follows.
What follows is the law, and it is not what was there before. There may have been some understanding between the various dominions with regard to such questions as the succession to the throne and matters of that kind, which have been adhered to by the British government but have not been mentioned in
our constitution, the British North America Act. No change can be made to the British North America Act except by legislation at Westminster. There may be some argument regarding the new state of things that has subsequently developed which could be settled by conferences between the British government and the governments of the dominions; but so far as our constitution is concerned, it is an act of the parliament at Westminster and can be changed only by the parliament at Westminster. It is like a municipal by-law which can be amended only by another by-law and not by a resolution of the municipal council.
I never believed in the pompous designation of "dominion". It is pompous. It was something to satisfy the pride of colonials. Either Canada is a realm, as his majesty described it in speaking to the senate, and the record of that statement is also contained in our own Hansard, or we are not a dominion but just a colony.
There is no definition of a dominion in the statute of Westminster. For a definition we have to go to a book that belongs to the house and is put on the Clerk's table for our perusal. It is called "The Concise Oxford Dictionary" and it is for the Clerk's table. When there is no definition of a word in the interpretation section of a statute we have to seek for its meaning in the dictionary, not a common dictionary, but the dictionary on the Clerk's table for the use of Mr. Speaker or the chairman of the committee of the whole house when we are sitting in committee. Now what do we find in the Oxford dictionary, for use at the table of the House of Commons? I .find this definition of "dominion":
Dominion. (Dominion of Canada, name given to Canadian colonies united 1867).
That is what the dictionary says. Therefore we cannot pretend to be anything more than a colony. It is precisely because some British lord was afraid of what the effect might be in the United States if Canada were called a kingdom that Canada was given the pompous, I repeat, and false name of a dominion.
The first section of this act reads:
In this act the expression "dominion" means any of the following dominions, that is to say, the Dominion of Canada, the Commonwrealth of Australia, the Dominion of New Zealand, the Union of South Africa, the Irish Free State and Newfoundland.
It is precisely because some of the other dominions, especially Australia, South Africa and Ireland objected, not to the definition but to the meaning of the designation "dominion", that these countries are called the Commonwealth of Australia, the Union of South Africa, and the Irish Free State. They objected to

the word "dominion" because it was a pompous designation for a colony. We should not go on stilts, Mr. Chairman, when we discuss external affairs and our status. There are some people, you know, who climb on stilts ,to appear greater than they are, and then after the speech is made, they drop down to earth again and become human beings. I now quote section 2 of the statute of Westminster:
(1)	The Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, shall not aply to any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament of a dominion.
(2)	No law and no provision of any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament . of a dominion shall be void or inoperative on the ground that it is repugnant to the law of England, or to the provisions of any existing or future act of parliament of the United Kingdom, or to any order, rule or regulation made under any such act, and the powers of the parliament of a dominion shall include the power to repeal or amend any such act, order, rule or regulation in so far as the same is part of the law of the dominion.
In other words, the statute of Westminster repeals the Colonial. Laws Validity Act of 1865. It means that since 1931 if our legislation is in conflict with that of Great Britain it will be in force just the same. Two or three years ago, in my weekly column in a Montreal daily, I said it would be very interesting to have a check-up made of each statute passed foy our parliament and by each legislature of this country from the time of the Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, until the passing of the statute of Westminster, 1931, and to compare each of our laws, both federal and provincial with each of the British statutes to see whether there was not some infringement somewhere. But nobody saw the joke. Moreover, I suggested that two senile judges who had been superannuated should start the work; they would have had to live as long as Methuselah to complete it.
Lett us take note of section 7:
(1)	Nothing in this aot shall be deemed to apply bo the repeal, amendment or alteration of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1930, or any order, rule or regulation made thereunder.
Therefore, sir, the statute of Westminster does not touch or change our constitution, the British North America Act, which remains the same. Then subsection 2:
(2)	The provisions of section two of this act shall^ extend to law's made foy any of the provinces of Canada and to the powers of the legislatures of such provinces.
Which means that the Colonial Laws Validity Act applies not only to dominion acts but also to provincial acts. Then subsection 3:
(3)	The powers conferred by this aot upon the parliament of Canada or upon the legislatures of the provinces shall he restricted to the enactment of law's in relation to matters

w'ithin the competence of the parliament of Canada or of any of the legislatures of the provinces respectively.	"
There is something extraordinary about section 3, which reads thus:
3.	It is hereby declared and enacted that the parliament of a dominion has full power to make laws having extra-territorial operation.
Yes, sir, that is very fine; but what is the use of having it when on the other hand the disallowance provisions of the British North America Act are left there, in virtue of which our legislation is sent to Westminster and the British government has two years to disallow our legislation? What freedom do we have now? Or, if "freedom" is a rather stronger expression than I intended, I will use the word "autonomy".
4.	No act of parliament of the United Kingdom passed after the commencement of this aot shall extend, or be deemed to extend, to a dominion as part of the law of that dominion, unless it _is^ expressly declared in that act that that dominion has requested, and consented to the enactment thereof.
That is fair. But it is important to note what is repeated in the two subsections of section 2 and also in section 4-and this is why there was something serious in my suggestion about the judges. All the legislation which has been passed by our parliament from 1865 to 1931 and by our provinces from the date of their creation until 1931 is null and void, and remains null and void notwithstanding the statute of Westminster if it comes in conflict with any British law. We know nothing of the past; a check-up should be made. I say that very seriously, because the statute of Westminster had no retroactive effect on the matter.
5.	Without prejudice to the generality of .the foregoing provisions of this act, sections seven hundred and thirty-five and seven hundred and thirty-six of the Merchant Shipping Aot 1894, shall be construed as though reference therein to the legislature of a British possession did not include reference to the parliament of a dominion.
6.	Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provisions of this aot, section four of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890, (which requires certain laws to be reserved for the signification of His Majesty's pleasure or to contain a suspending clause), and so much of section seven of that aot as requires the approval of His Majesty in Council to any rules of court for regulating the practice and procedure of a colonial court of admiralty, shall cease to have effect in any dominion as from the commencement of this aot.
The only difference between a so-called dominion and a colony is this, which we find in section 5, "Powers of dominion parliaments in relation to merchant shipping." I have read it. Afterwards there are sections which refer to dominions other than ours.
