The matter was discussed at full length on June 30, 1931. I have not time to read this debate, but to students of parliamentary history and constitutional law I say, if you desire to know the views expressed on that occasion by Mr. Bennett, Mr. Lapointe and Mr. Ralston, you have only to go to Hansard. The matter was discussed on other occasions, especially on March 10, 1939. I tell you that I find that the statute of Westminster is just a kind of fictitious propaganda, the instrument of a sort of amphibious gentleman, a labour lord-I cannot conceive of labour lords-Lord Passfield, better known as Sidney Webb.
In the first place I find that the name "statute of Westminster" is the summit of absurdity to designate one statute in particular. I had it in mind to put a question on the order paper. "Besides the two 'statutes of Westminster' passed in the years 1275 and 1285, 18 Edward I, chapter 1, and the 'Statute of Westminster' 1931, 22 George V., chapter 4, were there other statutes of Westminster? If so, what are they, and how many were passed between 18 Edward I and 22 George V., during several centuries?" All enactments from Westminster are statutes of Westminster; why pick out this one and call it the statute of Westminster? "We will give you freedom; we will give you autonomy." But we find that it is very much restricted. I have heard some young men talk about the autonomy of this country; they say, "The statute of Westminster has put it in force." But it means nothing, or practically nothing; it is just fictitious propaganda to give the inhabitants of the dominions the impression that they are always walking on stilts and that they are much greater than they are.
On March 10, 1939, there was a debate on the Gariepy bill, reported at pages 1782-4 of Hansard. Mr. Gariepy was then member for Three Rivers, and the object of his bill was to establish the anniversary of the statute of Westminster as a statutory'holiday. That was not enacted. On that occasion the late Mr. Lapointe spoke. He said:
It is the bond that binds together the various parts of the commonwealth under the same crown.
I do not believe that. I believe that the bond that unites all parts of the British empire is the British crown, and I do not see how the statute of Westminster could be substituted for the crown in uniting the various parts of the British empire or the British commonwealth, or whatever name you choose to give it.
Freedom is the cement that binds all these nations together .... The Statute of Westminster is a great step but it is not as final for Canada as it has been for most of the other
dominions because of certain things which prevented complete nationhood, in spite of the fact that those obstacles are of our own will, are there because we want them to be there.
These obstacles exist because we want them to exist, and if we are not autonomous it is because we do not want to be autonomous. He is referring to the amendment to the constitution.
First . . . how can it be accepted in international law that we are a fully sovereign nation when we have to resort to the parliament of another country to effect changes in our constitutional structure?
I fully agree with that. Now with regard
to the privy council:
Litigants from Canada must go to the mother country to get a final decision in Canadian cases.
I would be in favour of appeals to the privy council if the members of that tribunal were not also politicians, because they belong to the House of Lords. If the privy council were completely independent of politics, I would be for it. I would be for the continuation of our system, for a very simple reason. Everybody speaks of the independence of.judges. Judges should be like Caesar's wife, above every reproach. I have no objection to having a case decided in London any more than having international settlements made at Geneva. How can men who went to Geneva or to the Hague in Holland for the settlement of their disputes object to decisions being given by the privy council in London? I am opposed to it because those judges are politicians; they belong to the House of Lords. Otherwise they would be fully qualified to act as our final judges, and the question of cost is nothing, because there is so much provided for the office of the Canadian high commissioner in London that it would be possible to 'engage a couple of solicitors in London at $10,000 a year to submit all cases to the privy council.
We cannot say that we have complete equality of status and full sovereignty until we have a Canadian flag.
It is true that a flag is a symbol of sovereignty, but it must mean something. In my part of the country, when the framework of a building is finished, the custom and the tradition is to put the head of a pine tree on top, and that indicates to all those who pass by that, although the building is not completed, the framework
is.	But how can we put a flag in the air, like castles in Spain, when there is nothing there to support it? Only sovereign nations can have a flag. A flag must mean something, because if it means nothing, if it does not mean autonomy, I do not see why we should have
it.	That is my humble view. There must be a meaning to it, and so long as there is no
Supply-External Affairs

meaning we cannot have our flag. It is not a question of not being patriotic or being a good Canadian. I find that we have enough illusions with regard to the statute of Westminster and it is time to put a stop to them and to take things as they are. What would be of greater importance for us than having a flag would be to consider each piece of legislation in a truly Canadian spirit. Our legislation should have Canadian inspiration and not inspiration from outside. It would be much better to start at the bottom and then gradually climb to the top. Mr. Lapointe then went on to say:
The three matters I have mentioned will have to be dealt with and definitely solved before we can say that we are like the other dominions which have all done so.
They themselves, however, were subject to the illusion of autonomy in their constitutions. It was said that they could amend the constitutions themselves, but in each constitution there was provision for the disallowance of their legislation at Westminster. Where wouldl they go? If their amendment to their constitution should happen to displease Westminster, the British government can disallow it at any time within two years. The only country where that does not prevail is Eire.
Mr. Lapointe also spoke on March 31, 1939, on the question of neutrality with reference to the subject of a foreign policy. He is reported at page 2466 of Hansard. He spoke first of a common national status. We have no Canadian citizenship, and Canadian citizenship should come before the flag. Second, he referred to the use of the diplomatic and consular functions of Britain. I did not agree with the Prime Minister when he said that the new Canadian consul general in New York should work in close cooperation with the British officials over there. We may be in conflict with regard to trade and business, but conflict in regard to trade is emulation, not war, and the duty of the consul general in New York is not to receive instructions from the British ambassador or the British consul general, but to take instructions, from this government only, for the best interests of the country.
The third point to which Mr. Lapointe referred! was the foreign enlistment act; the fourth, the British preference, and the fifth, shipping legislation.
At the special session of 1939 he mentioned these matters and he is reported at page 66 of Hansard. What he said was this, in effect. For all these reasons, it is impossible for this country to be neutral. It shows also that we are not autonomous. And what I complain of is that this country is described as autonomous when it is not. I am making an argument now,
[Mr Pouliot.]
and I do not say to the imperialists that it is better to be autonomous than not to be, because I want them to have a restful weekend. But so long as we are not autonomous and so long as our legislation can be disallowed within two years by the British government, I do not see how we can say that we are free and are not under guardianship, and that we should have a flag. That flag should be at half-mast.
There are some other things, but I should like to see this country autonomous in fact. I mean by that, through legislation, as opposed to the many eloquent words that we hear from so many lips. In our national acts we should always proceed with the first thought for the interests of this country. In the second place we should not feel too much impressed by outsiders who' come here. At the present time some of our statesmen seem to have 'an unfortunate inferiority complex when outsiders are concerned. They consider that they are much better than Canadians simply because they come from outside the country. I am referring particularly to certain experts who have come here from Great Britain, the United States or other places.
Then there is another consideration, which was so well expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), about our taking part in the pan-American union. Most of us were bom in this country, and many of those who were not born here have become real Canadians; they want to make this country their own for themselves and for those who will come after them. All realize that the future of the world .will be mostly on this continent; I mean in the two Americas. I do not know how it will be taken, but I have a suggestion to make. I suggest that the motto of each part of the British empire, at least the colonies that are called dominions, should be the French motto of, "liberte, egalite, fraternite." By liberty I mean autonomy in legislation under the British crown. What fraternity do we practise with the other dominions? There is one dominion which has been given the cold shoulder.
I do not intend to argue this point, but when the war is over it will be over for the neutrals as well as for those who have been at war. In my humble opinion the duty of Canada, which has been doing so much for other countries, immediately after the w$r will be to do everything possible for Ireland, not only for Eire but for Northern Ireland as well. Help should be given to this dominion because they are the closest to us; they are between us and England and Scotland.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know of no more important debate that could take place in this parliament than one concerning the relationship of Canada to other parts of the empire and our foreign relations generally. I am sure that all of us were impressed to-day by the optimistic tone of the Prime Minister's speech in so far as the war situation is concerned. As he spoke I coupled his remarks with the indication he gave the other day that we in Canada, in common with other parts of the empire, are on the eve of tremendous developments on the battle fronts. The right hon. gentleman gave the warning that in the near future the blood of our own kith and kin will be shed wherever the invasion is commenced. It was not by the statute of Westminster, which merely placed in statute form the status of the component parts of this empire, nor by the Balfour declaration of 1926 that Canada gained a position of equality with other parts of the empire; it was gained by the sacrifice and service of those who gave their all in the last war, and is being maintained at this moment by the service of those who are in the armed forces in this war.
What I have to say to-day is not comprised in any set speech. Anything I have prepared has been prepared during the day and represents the results of some thought given to matters of foreign policy and our relations within the empire over a period of years.
There are few Canadians who have any illusions that this nation will be able to remain neutral or isolated or adopt an attitude of being uninterested in foreign affairs during the years to come. In spite of the speeches that one sometimes hears made, such as the one made not so long ago by a member of another house, Canadians as a whole appreciating their membership in the British empire have no desire to depart from that relationr ship. They are prepared to accept not only that relationship but the responsibility of cooperation with and assistance to other parts of the empire in the years to come. The opposition believes and I quote:
That the guarantee of freedom, security and opportunity for Canadians will be found in the strengthening of the British commonwealth, its closer association with the United States and the other allies in this war and in the application of the principles of the Atlantic charter.
Canadian unity is dependent upon the continuance of Canada as a part of the British commonwealth. One could not imagine the various races and creeds in this country, the existence of rights and of responsibilities as between those various peoples comprising Canada, in any other relationship than within the empire, bound together in the empire by a spirit of loyalty and affection to the crown.
I was disappointed that the Prime Minister did not deal with the matter, although he has made reference to it in the past. Having regard to international transportation and communications by air, and having regard to the fact that the circumference of the world has shrunk to the point where no nation is distant from any other nation to-day more than sixty hours, with the result that international non-cooperation, isolation or separatism can no longer constitute a policy for the nation, we must look forward to the postwar problems that the Prime Minister says are now engaging the attention of certain committees to the end that in the post-war development Canada as the centre of the universe in the new air maps which are being issued will take her proper place within this empire in advancing civil aviation.
Before I deal with that I wish to make a few general observations. I believe that in recent years we have learned one thing, as was so well expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) in his speech this morning. Canada can no longer take a negative foreign policy attitude. Her attitude from now on must be one of a positive nature. Our interests in foreign affairs geographically parallel those of the United States, and we
Supply-External Affairs

are bound to the crown by history and tradition. The crown symbolizes the common unity, the common purpose, the common concept of institutions based on freedom and liberty. The United States of America, as a nation friendly to us and a nation whose cooperation means so much to the empire and to Canada has many problems in common with ours. To those who say the day of annexation is here, I say they do not represent the viewpoint of the Canadian people; for on this continent there is ample room for two great nations, one a free and independent member of the British commonwealth, the other the Republic of the United States of America, joined together in close association.
The Prime Minister himself must feel a source of satisfaction in the development of the relations between Canada and the United States which has occurred during the period that he has been in public life as Prime Minister or as leader of the opposition. When we look at the development since the last war; when we look at the development since this w'ar began, we realize the changes that have taken place. I believe we must have a degree of unity in this country in connection with foreign affairs to a greater extent than in matters particularly affecting us within the nation. When one looks at the picture, Ogdensburg, Hyde Park, Casablanca and Washington, one realizes that each of those conferences has represented a milestone in the mobilization of the power of the Englishspeaking nations, not only for purposes of making war but for mutual development in times of peace, as is evidenced by the Atlantic charter.
I have already mentioned that Canada will hold a central position when this war is over. Having regard to the fact that the Prime Minister of Great Britain has said that Canada is the linchpin joining together the British commonwealth and the United States of America, to-day the air centre of the world, is it too much to hope for that when the peace conference convenes it should convene in the city of Ottawa, the centre of the world to-day on the air routes of the world and the interpreter of the will of the British people to the United States of America and also the interpreter of the United States of America to the people of Britain. However, it has not always been so. The war changed the attitude of the government of Canada, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I am not sure yet, Mr. Chairman, that we are far enough along the road to a positive policy in foreign affairs, nor have we sufficiently established our future position toward the British empire. Why have we to-day no imperial war council? Why have we to-day

no imperial war conferences? Why did Canada in the years before the war refuse to join the committee for imperial defence? If Canada had taken the attitude in 1935 and 1936, and up to the outbreak of the war, that she takes to-day; if she had let the world and the aggressor nations know then what her stand would be should war come, would the result have been different? That will always remain an enigma of history.
Canada prior to the war had refrained from participating in affairs affecting the welfare of this empire as a whole. I am referring now to a book that was referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South, "The British Commonwealth at War". At page 63 I find the following:
Since the war of 1914-18 representatives of Australia and New Zealand have frequently been present at the meetings of the committee and have asked for and received advice on .their defence problems. The other dominions, such as Canada, at least in recent years, refrained for political reasons from attending meetings of the committee.

speechtext: Who wrote that?

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
It is by Mr. H. Duncan Hall, of the British committee at Washington. He goes on to point out, too, in regard to an imperial war cabinet, that Mr. Churchill wants such an institution set up, and that he has asked for it. He refers to it in his book on two occasions, first at page 35 where he quotes the Prime Minister of Great Britain as saying the following on June 24, 1941:
As I have told the house, we very much desire such a conference.
And later on, at page 36 he says this:
"We have always been ready to form an imperial cabinet containing the Prime Ministers of the four dominions.' Unfortunately, he continued, it had not been possible for all of them to be present at one and the same time; ... In the last three months the Australian government, he pointed out, had been represented on the war cabinet by Sir Earle Page. The British government had now agreed to the specific requests of the Australian and New Zealand governments, that their accredited representatives should have the "right to be heard in the war cabinet in the formulation and direction of policy;" and similar facilities would be available to Canada and South Africa.
If that correctly represents the situation I would ask the Prime Minister why it is Canada adopts an attitude against becoming a member of this war cabinet in London, in order to participate in directing and controlling the war effort of the empire.
When Mr. Eden was here he was asked a question regarding the matter of a war cabinet,

Supply-External Affairs
or a war council, and the following report of the interview appeared in the Toronto Star as follows:
Questioned as to the advisability of an empire war council, a move which Premier King has opposed, Mr. Eden glanced toward the Canadian Prime Minister before he replied. Then he said: "My own direct experience is that we've got pretty good' machinery for integration of our war effort.
Then, these are the pertinent words:
Of course, if it can be improved, that would be all the better.
Then he turned, smiling .to Mr. King and joked: "I think I did pretty well on that one, don't you?" The Canadian Premier nodded approval.

speechtext: I do not agree that such is the inference at all.

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
That is my conclusion; and I point out, too, that throughout the period from 1925 on, Canada has taken the attitude of non-participation in these conferences, and has taken the stand that she ought not actively to participate in giving counsel and advice.
But it is said that these things are changed now. The question I ask is this: Are they changed? Only recently an article published on March 18, 1943, by Mr. Chester Bloom, Washington correspondent, said this in part:
Much of the readiness with which the dominions have followed the mother country's lead, however, has been due to the dire and immediate peril with which Hitler threatened the whole civilized world. Now that it begins to be clear that Germany cannot win the war, no matter how long the nazis may prolong it, and how much blood and treasure must yet be expended, the British statesmen are beginning to feel the lack of some unified British commonwealth agreement on international policy.
It is a fact that, irrespective of the visits from time to time of representatives of Canada and other parts of the empire, and despite the communications which no doubt take place several times a day, nevertheless no relationship equals that of a conference, when men put their feet under the table together, and discuss affairs together.
That is why I again bring to the Prime Minister's attention representations we have made before that Canada now, if only for the psychological effect on our people, and the people of the empire as a whole, should agree
to the setting up of that council, and to the sending of representatives to Great Britain, or wherever else the council may be convened.
In the last war there were delays in setting up the imperial war council. I believe the first imperial war council did not meet until the spring of 1917, at the same time as the imperial conference of that year. There were delays. But a reading of Sir Robert Borden's memoirs leads to one conclusion, and that is that when the time was darkest, when the submarine menace was worst, and when these statesmen came from all parts of the empire to Great Britain the effect of the Canadian troops overseas and on the people of Great Britain was such that it resulted in a greater determination, a great incentive to fight the war to victory.
The Prime Minister referred to this matter himself on February 17, 1941, when he said, as reported at page 812 of Hansard:
Direct consultations have been and may continue to be necessary from time to time. They, however, are likely to be most required concerning aspects of the common war effort which necessitate detailed inquiry. Five members of the present government have already visited the United Kingdom since the outbreak of the war. Their visits have been of the greatest assistance to the government in coordinating our war effort with the war effort of the United Kingdom.
That may be true. Those visits coordinated the war effort. If they had that beneficial result, would there not also be a vastly greater beneficial result if to-morrow morning it were announced that we in Canada are going to join the other parts of the empire in what might be called a victory gathering of an imperial war cabinet, and that we were to be represented by Canada's own Prime Minister?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
will now summarize what I was saying before the recess. I was making a plea for greater collaboration with the other nations of the empire through the formation of an imperial war cabinet in order to unite more strongly the peoples of the empire. While it might be said that as a result of the developments of science and of scientific means of communication, the prime ministers of the various parts of the empire are enabled to communicate with one another and thereby make unnecessary the convening of a war cabinet, I
Supply-External Affairs

would point out that the human touch is lacking in these communications. Churchill and Roosevelt having the same oportunities to use modern means of communication for getting in touch with each other nevertheless avail themselves of personal meeting in the interest of their respective countries.
I pass now for a moment to our relationship with the United States of America. Recently I had the privilege of being present in Ottawa when members of the various parliaments of the empire met informally with members of the United States congress, and there for the first time I learned how important it was to have such an opportunity of getting together and of ascertaining through an interchange of ideas that, after all, our problems at the present time bear a striking similarity to one another. If there is one thing more important than another to-day it is this, that anything that may cause cleavages between Canada and the United States must be avoided, that frankness should characterize all our relations and that a free exchange of ideas is the finest means known to avoid suspicion arising.
I wish to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister with a view to getting an answer thereon the situation prevailing today not only along the Alaska highway but in other parts of this dominion where representatives of the United States, in a community of interest with us, are stationed with a view to the improvement of the defences i of our country and of North America as a whole. Last year I had an opportunity of visiting the Alaska highway and of being in the town of White Horse and there meeting with the troops of the United States of America. I can say this, that I have never seen a finer body of men than these troops representing the United States-men in a foreign land and yet at all times conducting themselves in a way that brings credit to themselves and to the nation they represent. As a result of their being in Canada a reference was recently made to the supreme court with regard to their liability to Canadian law. I am not going to refer to that matter because it is now being considered by the court, except to say that the court has been asked for an opinion on a question which reads as follows:
Are members of the military or naval forces of the United States of America who are present in Canada with the consent of the government of Canada for purposes of military operations in connection with or related to the state of war now existing exempt from criminal proceedings prosecuted in Canadian criminal courts and, if so, to what extent and in what circumstances ?

The stand taken by the United States is that their troops in our country are not subject to the criminal law. There is, however, another matter which I think requires interpretation from the Minister for External Affairs, namely, in connection with a United States order that was issued on June 7, 1943. It is singularly of interest that this order should have been made, and I want to ask whether or not it applies to Canadians or British subjects who are employed by contractors in connection with work on the Alaska highway. I quote:
Paragraph 1 of Northwest Service Command General Orders No. 23, dated June 7, 1943, subject: _ ''United States military jurisdiction over civilians in Northwest Service Command" is quoted for the information of all concerned: "Regardless of citizenship, civilian employees of the United States government, or of contractors, working under and in physical proximity to the United States army, including those United States citizens in the above categories discharged from their employment who are awaiting transportation to the United States, are subject to military law and discipline under Article of War 2 (d)."
Does that mean that Canadians who are working for contractors under or in proximity to the United States army in Canada are subject only to military law? That is a matter which I think should be clarified. It has been brought to my attention by civilians so employed, and creates a striking situation in view of the attitude taken by the Prime Minister respecting Britain's right to operate air training schools on Canadian soil. It is true that was before the war, on July 1, 193S. I think it merits an interpretation by the Prime Minister and also an explanation of the circumstances under which it was brought into effect.
There was one matter with which the Prime Minister did not deal, and in the few moments at my disposal I intend to deal with it. He stated that committees had been set up for the purpose of considering postwar problems. One of the main problems affecting Canada as a member of the British empire, and by itself, and also our relations with the united nations is the question of post-war aviation. In to-day's press is a dispatch from Washington, July 8, reading as follows:
Discussions among British commonwealth countries on the broad subject of post-war aviation are being proposed by the British government, it was reported here to-day.
The meeting, likely to be held in London, would precede any aviation conference among the united nations. For some time it has been reported here that plans were under way to hold informal discussions soon-probably in Ottawa-among	representatives of Canada,
Britain, the United States and perhaps Russia

Supply-External Affairs
and China. However, anj plans to this effect may have to be modified if the London conference is held.
As yet we in, ithis parliament have had no information with regard to this meeting. On April 2 the Prime Minister made a statement on the subject, wherein he stated in part as follows, as reported in Hansard, at page 1777:
The problems of international air transport are, of course, immense and cannot be solved by one country. We are determined, however, that our influence on the course of events will be in the direction of international cooperation and collaboration. The Canadian government is in complete agreement with the United Kingdom government that "some form of international collaboration will be essential if the air is to be developed in the interests of mankind as a whole, trade served, international understanding fostered and international security gained."
A study of evamts following the treaty of Versailles and at the time of the treaty leads one to believe that many of the difficulties which took place among the then allied nations would have been avoided had there been conferences prior to the peace treaty and during the progress of the war. Aviation is one of the most outstanding problems affecting this nation and this empire. During the last three years, in the development of the commonwealth air training scheme, Canada has become the schoolroom of the British empire in the matter of aviation. I realize that with a war on and far from ended, the main problem before us is that of the war. At the same time post-war aviation is a subject which should receive the consideration Of parliament now and not be left to be considered solely by committees set up by the ministers.
The question of post-war airways is one of major concern. There have been few agreements made by Canada with respect to air rights and air transportation, and there are none, according to a return brought down, in answer to questions I asked some time ago, on May 24, which are valid "beyond the duration of the war or a short time after, or have any effect upon the control of international air routes or the operation of international or [DOT] commercial air lines after the conclusion of the war." That is a quotation from page one of the return. The only pre-war agreement which seems to be binding on all is a multilateral agreement made on May 27, 1936, between Canada, the Irish Free State, Newfoundland and the United Kingdom respecting transatlantic air services. A summary of that agreement was given by the then Minister of Transport on July 30, 1936, and I am not going to refer to it. Canada occupies a situation of
strategic importance in the post-war development. Prior to the war a question for consideration of several imperial conferences was the establishment of strategic naval bases. After this war a major consideration will be the establishment of strategic air bases as well. The polar projection maps show definitely that the air will be the future transportation medium in large measure after the war, and 'that the great transportation services of the future will be air-borne craft the size of which no one can now conceive.
What stand are we to take? What is our attitude to be? The matter comes under the jurisdiction of the Prime Minister, but I feel that the members of this house and the country at large are entitled to have information now as to what conferences are taking place and what attitude Canada will take at these conferences.
I suggest that consideration shouldl be given now, with the collaboration of the United States and the other allied nations, to the organization of a British commercial air transport line, to commence operations after the end of the war, by which a world-girdling organization will be established, with each nation within the empire retaining its own domestic routes.
When the history of this war is written it may well be that Hitler's misconception of the character of the British commonwealth was one of the great mistakes which he made. He believed that without bonds of iron binding the empire together it would fall asunder; he did not realize the fact that what binds it together is the crown and the imponderables which go with British citizenship. I am going to quote in that connection the statement of Mr. Churchill some five months before the war, when, with that prescience which has characterized his statesmanship throughout, he used these words:
Some foreigners mock at the British empire because there are no parchment bonds or hard steel shackles which compel its united action. But there are other forces far more compulsive to which the whole fabric spontaneously responds. These deep tides are flowing now. They sweep away in their flow differences of class and party. They override the vast ocean spaces which separate the dominions of the king.
I feel that if there is one thing we should do at this time it is to lay the foundations for welding together, still closer than ever before, the bonds of empire, and I know of no means whereby that can be effected to a greater extent, without antagonizing those of the united nations who to-day are engaged in the
Supply-External Affairs

common effort and crusade, than by the consideration of the development of an empire air scheme. Individual members of the empire cannot do it by themselves.
The Prime Minister has made a declaration with respect to the Trans-Canada Air Lines. He states that they will operate without opposition, that in so far as feeder routes are concerned they will be, I presume, under private initiative and control. We have to-day across Canada a vast number of airports. We have trained tens of thousands of pilots who move forward to all parts of the world in an ever-increasing stream.
We have all the facilities for a world air organization. We have men who, when the war is over, will return trained as airmen were never trained before, and in the development of an air scheme such as I suggest, employment would be given to many of these men, use would be made of our airports and facilities, and the bonds of empire would be strengthened.
The question arises, how could it be governed? We have the board of transport commissioners. We could set up a board such as that, with representatives of each of the governments affected within the empire. We cannot develop a world-girdling air institution here in Canada by ourselves and without cooperation. If we look at it from the purely narrow .point of view of expediency, Canada has too small a population to maintain her vast domestic set-up in connection with air transportation, and to maintain as well a world air system after the war. Other parts of the empire are very much in the same position. Nor could we individually maintain the necessary aircraft production or continue the operation of such a vast scheme. But together, and in unity of purpose, the nations of the empire, without antagonizing the other united nations, could maintain powerful air routes in all parts of the world, the bases now established permitting of the development and expansion of such an all-empire route.
Canada has an important place to take in the post-war period. Canada can never return to the days before the war, the days when we did not as individual Canadians interest ourselves as we ought to have done in the world about us. Canada can never return to its pre-war position after the vast expansion in industry that has taken place in this country during the war. There is no more important subject now for the post-war than a declaration from the Prime Minister setting forth the attitude that Canada will take, and giving to the other parts of this empire the promise that when this war is over, in the interests of

world trade and world peace, the air facilities of all parts of the empire will be devoted to the welfare of mankind.
I have not- endeavoured to-day to introduce anything of a partisan nature. Our foreign affairs and our attitude to the empire must, I believe, be founded upon the wishes, desires and aspirations of our people, dedicated to the end that we as an empire, when this war is over, will so gird ourselves that the new world will be free from the blights of fear, international and national.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lethbridge (M-r. Blackmore), earlier in the day, said th'at the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), by saying little, had satisfied everybody on the foreign policy of Canada. I do no.t know about everybody, but certainly one may judge by the speeches that have been rendered in the later part of the afternoon that he did not succeed in satisfying hon. members opposite. However, 1 do not believe that they represent the majority of Canada, in their view. The Prime Minister of Canada, in the views he has expressed not only to-day, but on previous occasions, has succeeded in representing that majority view batter .than anyone else in the recant history of our country.
Any one who listened to the speeches to-day, or some of them, at any rate, would wonder how Canada had a foreign policy at all or even whether there is a country -called Canada. I wish to assure my hon. friends tha-t there is a country called Canada. It is a good country; it is the country we are fighting to preserve; and yet to-day we had -the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) advancing the doctrine, which was new to me, that he -could not imagine the ra-ces of Canada, the peoples in the various divisions of Canada, getting on together in any other -relationship than within -the empire, though a little later he said tha-t Canada is the centre of the world. It is very difficult to reconcile these and other points of view exjpressed to-day.
We have had a number of interesting speeches, and there is a great deal in them with which every one -of us can agree. But I find in- some of them -curious mixtures of reality and myth. There is reality about the nature of the world we are living in, but something stops and fails to carry over the speaker to see completely the consequences of that reality. I suggest that what has stopped these speakers from, being consistent and right is a mistaken conception of the British empire, a conception which- is not in accord with reality.

Supply

External Affairs
Lest I be misunderstood in any of the views I am now going to express, let me say with the most complete sincerity that no one could more fully appreciate what the British people have done in this war. I believe that in four respects the record of Britain has been extraordinary.
In the first place they had political institutions which are perhaps their greatest gift to civilization and which even worked in the moment of crisis, in the supreme hour of trial, to replace Mr. Chamberlain by Mr. Churchill. And I may say here that as far back as 1937 I was one of the few people who pursued the unpopular course in Canada of advocating the replacement of Mr. Chamberlain by Mr. Churchill at a time when it was most difficult to advocate that course. In the second place, under Mr. Churchill's leadership the British people held out and literally saved the world. In the third place, they produced the best planes and possibly one of the greatest fighting instruments the world has ever seen in the eighth army. In the fourth place, from the low watermark of centuries in the early months of 1940 they built themselves up to heights which will be the admiration of decent people for all time.
In paying this tribute do not let it be thought for one moment that I am forgetting the contribution made to our cause by Russia, although Russia gained time as a result of the defence put up by Britain. Before that China had given us time by her bitter struggle and sacrifice for so many years.
Having said this, may I be just a little technical for a moment. The empire, properly so-called, is the United Kingdom and the colonial empire. The commonwealth is the United Kingdom and the self-governing dominions of Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Canada and whatever division Eire may be in. The nations of the commonwealth, apart from the United Kingdom, have nothing to do with the government of the empire and nothing to do with the government of each other, except in so far as there is still the vestigal remains of the lack of autonomy to which the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) referred to-day. They are there because we choose to have them. No one in Canada or elsewhere can take any pleasure from rattling the chains of subordination because, if we have ties of that kind1, we have them because we want them.
We work together when it is in our interest to do so, and it usually is. The conception which most interests Canadians is not that of the British empire vis-a-vis the world; it is of
the nations of the British commonwealth working with the world. I suggest to hon. members of this committee that in this distinction there is a considerable difference between some hon. members opposite and myself. I believe that my conception of the British commonwealth and what it means and what it can do for the world is a nobler one than theirs. I believe that mine is more in accord with reality, and with the interest and welfare of all of us. I believe it is more inspiring because it is based on the principle of freedom and on responsibility which is a correlative of freedom.
If because of ties of affection, tradition, literature and common political institutions, all symbolized in a common crown, the independent and autonomous nations of the British empire are drawn together so that they have a policy which is coincident, that is a much finer and more helpful thing than if we all had a policy which was arrived at in some other way by reason of our having only one voice, as was advocated by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). Our strength is in the freedom with which we are associated. Other nations will be more ready to work with that strength as we make them see and recognize that freedom. In that connection I differ fundamentally from the hon. member for Vancouver South. The conception I have of the British commonwealth is an association of free nations working together-

I am discussing the matter of having one voice, which was the phrase used by my hon. friend. The point I am making is that the way we arrive at that one voice is of fundamental importance, not only to us but to the nations of the world with whom we are associated. I suggest to my hon. friend and to this committee that the nations of the world will appreciate us and our value, and we shall have far greater influence if we can have a common voice from a consideration of our own interests rather than if we always speak with a single voice and have a single policy on every point.
The correlation of freedom is responsibility. But responsibility to whom? Obviously in

Supply-External Affairs

Canada we are not responsible to the people of South Africa, we are not responsible to the people of any other commonwealth country, we are responsible to the people of Canada. What brought us here, what brought our forefathers here, and why we aim to have our sons live here after us, is that we have an affection and devotion and loyalty to Canada.
Against this background may I consider the suggestion made by the hon. member for Lake Centre that there should be an imperial conference and an imperial war cabinet during the war. That has been discussed on a great many occasions in this house and elsewhere. My objections to it are twofold. In the first place, it is not practicable as a regular routine. The greatest usefulness any dominion prime minister or the Prime Minister of Great Britain can have is to lead his own nation in the fight against the aggressors, to direct the efforts of his own people. When it might be possible for Field Marshal Smuts and Mr. Fraser to go to London, it might not be possible for the Prime Minister of Canada and Mr. Curtin to go. It simply is not practicable to arrange to have an imperial war committee meet in London as a matter of regular routine throughout the war.
The first duty of the prime ministers of the commonwealth is to their own nations; they can make their greatest contribution to the common cause in their own nations. From time to time they may be able to meet with other leaders to discuss specific points, but the possibility of regular routine meetings by all of them is ruled out by the practical considerations to which I have referred.
Further, the experience of one commonwealth prime minister indicates a valid objection to the course to which the hon. member for Lake Centre has directed his evidence. I refer to Mr. Menzies who was away from his country so long that when he got back he found himself in a position in which he was defeated. It is impossible in these days of rapidly moving events and grave issues for any group of prime ministers to be out of their countries for any considerable length of time, to make decisions affecting their countries and be sure of being able to implement them on their return.

important consideration; the British commonwealth at the present time has no special interest distinct from that of the other nations fighting on our side. The interest of the United States in all the affairs in which we are interested is identical with ours. Their interest is in mobilizing the utmost strength to defeat the aggressor. It is the same as ours. We have no distinct interest in the British commonwealth at this time which differentiates us from the United States with regard to doing right throughout the world or which differentiates the United Kingdom from Russia in the fight in Europe, or China from Australia, New Zealand and Canada with regard to the struggle against Japan.
I would have supported my hon. friend if he had said we need additional agencies in the united nations to combine our strength to greater advantage than has been done up to now. I believe in time it will be found necessary to work out some system of combined strategy for Europe such as has been worked out in other centres of the world. Any system of cooperation will have to involve representation in some way or another of all the forces fighting on a particular front. But running all through the statements of my hon. friends opposite, of the hon. member for Lake Centre, the hon. member for Broadview and the hon. member for Lethbridge is, I believe, the conception of the interest of the British empire or British commonwealth as being separate and distinct from that of the interest of the rest of the world.

But I do not agree that they are synonymous, for the reasons which I have stated. I should remind my hon. friend that I said I was speaking technically when I described the position of the British empire.
At this moment in history it is the triumph of the members of the British Commonwealth that they have no special interest. Their interests are the same as those of other nations fighting the aggressors. If this is accepted bj7 us it means that we have a conception of the British Commonwealth which will be welcomed by all other nations. We should appreciate that when one of the British peoples refers to the other British peoples in terms of affection, the majority of the people of the world do not have the same degree of attachment to the British Commonwealth or Empire as British citizens have.
Let us look for a moment at the purpose of foreign policy. What is it? The purpose of foreign policy of any country is to pursue the interests of that country. The purpose of the foreign policy of Britain is to pursue the interests of Britain; the purpose of the foreign policy of the United States is to pursue the interests of the United States; and any prime minister who did not pursue what was conceived to be the interests of his country would be turned out of office. Of course it should be made plain to the people, with the growing development of affairs, that the interest of a country is bound up with the interest of every other country. But still the purpose of any national policy and foreign policy is to serve the interest of that country. That is true of Canada as it is true of every other nation. What is the interest of Canada? It is, of course, to secure the security and prosperity of the Canadian people. We do not differ from any other country in our foreign policy; we do not differ from any of the countries with whom we are fighting as allies, to pursue security and prosperity. But when we seek to see how that is to be done we get into practical questions of some difficulty. There is one first step on which we all agree; that is, that we must win the war, and we must realize that, for us in Canada the time of greatest strain and sacrifice lies ahead. Second, we must recognize that what we are fighting for is the defeat of aggression. The sanctity of individual life. The chance to have a good life is not only our aim in war but also our aim in peace.
And we are helping to-day to make the conditions of peace. Everything we do in this or any other country is setting the framework of the post-war world. We may be sure that
72537-291J
there will be no new heaven or new earth except in so far as we make it to-day oi later by our united work. It lies in our hands to make it. It is only the part of wisdom to look ahead and try to learn from what is happening here as well as in the peculiar past to which the hon. member for Broadview referred.
The interest of the people of Canada in foreign policy is not academic. It is measured by 750,000 men in the armed forces, and by our harnessing our whole resources to defeat the enemy. It is shown in peace by the farmers in Saskatchewan, who know that the amount of money they have in their pockets will depend on world trade, world markets and world security. The war has brought out that 'the world is one. That is brought home to us by our place on the main roads of the air to Europe and Asia. It was brought home to us when five tired Canadian boys got off a plane on a summer night last year at Uplands after bombing Germany that morning. That cracked old conceptions of the world. The war has shown us that no nation is far enough away to keep out of a major war or strong enough to fight one alone. This applies to Russia and to the United States as well as to Britain; it also applies to Canada.
The hon. member for Lethbridge suggested that we should arm ourselves to the teeth in order to defend Canada. He then suggested that we should do so in conjunction with the other parts of the British commonwealth. I want to have not only the Strength of the British commonwealth at my back in the world that lies ahead; in the world that lies ahead I want to have the strength of all the nations of the world organized into a community at my back, because there is no other way to prevent aggression.

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext: Would the hon. member tell us how much he would like to contribute, and in what way he would like to contribute to that strength he so admirably wishes to have at his back?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
I would contribute our full share, as we are doing in the war. I would contribute our full share, whatever it may be. And because Canada has a special place in the world I would contribute more than what seemed to be our share. I would go the full limit, because we have a greater stake in security than almost any other nation. We have a finer country and we want to preserve it. We want to preserve our way of life here.
The only way to organize strength is by collective action. Surely it is obvious that if you have collective action you have to have collective instruments to direct the use of that collective strength. We are gradually building up those instruments during the war, through the instrumentalities of the united nations. We ought to try for faster progress in this, while we are united in the common purpose of defeating the enemy. If we get the habit of cooperation during the war, and develop the machinery that will work during a war, then we gradually move into the period of peace afterwards. But unless this is done during the war, then there is less chance of doing it after. '
To-day the realities of geography establish that the world is one, that peace is indivisible, and also, as the Prime Minister said, prosperity is indivisible, too. The prosperity of every part of Canada depends upon the prosperity of every other part. We cannot have people in Ottawa, in Saint John, in Saskatchewan, prosperous, without other people in Canada being prosperous. The same applies throughout the world, to even a greater degree, because Canada has become more dependent on international trade during the war than she was even before the war. We can only support our standard of living, our national income, our prosperity-because that is what it is-if after the war conditions are secure through international action which will enable us to exchange our goods and services with other nations to about the same degree as we are doing during the war.
We can have security and prosperity internal and external, but we cannot have just security or just prosperity. And we cannot have it here

and not somewhere else. It has all to go together. I suggest that not only is that lesson taught and preached by people like Mr. Willkie in his book "One World", but that it is coming to be the common idea among all the peoples of the world. They are awaking to the reality of it. A country like Canada can make a very considerable contribution towards this end. We can make it as a member of the British commonwealth of nations, and we can make it in working with other nations. The members of the British commonwealth of nations can make a great contribution. But we cannot make so effective a contribution if we have to speak with one voice. While we should try by consultation to have a common policy, we should not have a single policy, which is quite a different thing. The difference is fundamental to the concept of the world before us, and of the British commonwealth as I have tried to describe them.
If the 'British commonwealth were always to speak with only one voice to the rest of the world, then you would have the British commonwealth set off against the yorld, and the commonwealth countries would not be able to make their separate contributions to its welfare. Unity of this kind would defeat its own end. For example, you could not then have Canada join the pan-American Union, in the way the hon. member for Vancouver South suggested. The nations of the commonwealth can have far more influence if they happen to work together as five, six or seven nations than if they are one.
And also, this idea of a single foreign policy is unworkable. Who would declare the foreign policy? I am sure no prime minister or no government in England would agree that its foreign policy was to be determined by Canada or by Australia. They would not agree to it. Their interests are too- serious to permit them to agree to it. We could not agree to it, either. But we should consult together, of course. In -consequence of that consultation and in consequence of our common traditions and common interests we may arrive at policies which are -the same. That may happen in nine cases out o-f ten, and when it does it will be -more effective than if we struck out as a solid unit.
So that I suggest to my hon. friends that it is not in the interests of the British commonwealth of nations, or any member of it, that we should seek to have a single voice in foreign policy. Everyone agrees that we should work together with members of the commonwealth and other nations just as we are doing. I do not conceive of the commonwealth as being a sort of concentration of

Supply-External Affairs
power of a collective character, such as my hon. friends seem to think it is. I think of it as a great association which has contributed. much to the world, and will contribute more. But its very lifeblood is freedom. And the very principle of freedom, which gives it its character, and which keeps us part of it, demands that we should be free to determine ou.r own policy.
Then, also, we should determine our own policy because that is the only way in which we can get support for any policy in Canada. No one could get support in Canada for a policy determined from outside of Canada. In Canada we should seek to have a policy which would lead this country to take a most active part in the affairs of the world, because that is our interest. Our interest in the affairs of the world to-day is not exceeded by that of any other country; our power is, but not our interest. The best way to get the unity of feeling among our own people, which is the necessary basis of a foreign policy, is that it should be a foreign policy which is based on Canada's interests, and appeal to Canadians as Canadians.

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext: When the hon. member speaks about Canada's interest, does he mean self-interest?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext: Of course, self-interest.

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext: We have no obligations to the rest of the world, then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Of course we have.
Everything I have said should show my hon. friend that we have an obligation to the rest of the world, just as the rest of the world has an obligation to us. When I speak of self-interest I naturally assume the hon. member to think I meant enlightened self-interest; because our interest is not a selfish interest; it cannot be. We are interested in a world in which small nations will be secure. We cannot secure that condition by ourselves. We can secure it only by working together with other nations, and making our full contribution toward the common pool of security and prosperity.
This concept of the relationship was described by Lionel Curtis in his book Civitas Dei, written in 1937. Mr. Curtis is no separatist, as my hon. friends know, and he says:
I am thus led to state a conclusion from which I have long shrunk. In spite of all that is said and written and of all appearances, the dominion have not as yet acquired the character of national commonwealths, and cannot acquire it until they have accepted in unequivocal terms the responsibility for peace or war. They cannot do this, nor feel they have done it, until
they have notified to the world at large that they are not involved in war till their own governments have officially declared that they are so involved.
The cabinet, parliament and electorate of a dominion which had once come to this point would begin to take an interest in world affairs to which they cannot be brought in times of peace, so long as the present conditions exist. They would cease to be screened from the hard facto by direct contact with which men learn what those facte are. They would have to provide for themselves the diplomatic machinery without which no government can follow the course of foreign affairs. They would lose the habit of mind induced by a satellite position- the habit of mind which prevents them from seeing the key position which they hold at this juncture of human history.
This statement was true in 1937 and has been proved to be true not only by the course of events since and by the participation of Canada in the war as the separate act of her i vn government authorized by her own parliament, but also by this discussion. We can only have a foreign policy which is unequivocal when we arrive at a foreign policy from considerations which are based on Canadian sentiments and Canadian interests. Among the first of those interests one would naturally say was the survival of Britain as in Canada's interest. It is important that we should recognize that we are fighting in this war because it is in Canada's interest to see the survival of Britain and ourselves rather than that we should fight automatically just because Britain is involved.
My hon. friend the member for Vancouver South suggested that there is danger of our getting a small nation complex. I must say that I do not know what a small nation complex is. But if a big power complex means that a power seeks to dominate someone else, and if a small nation complex is the opposite of that and means a desire to work together in harmony, I am all for it.

maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext: Does the hon. member believe that it is the destiny of Canada to be always a small nation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, Canada has great possibilities of growth, but the soundest foundation for the growth of Canada is in a conception of our country which all Canadians can share. That is fundamental to our progress. In the extremes of isolation, on the one hand, and a wrong conception of Canada's relationship with the empire, on the other hand we have extremes which make it extraordinarily difficult for us to have a united country and a united policy, although the people between the two extremes undoubtedly represent the great majority of the people of this country.
Supply-External Affairs

Speaking about small powers, Sir William Beveridge writing in The Observer said this, which I think will answer my hon. friend's question:
At the end of the last war, -the aim was phrased by some as making the world safe for democracy. But democracy is a means, not an end. The aim for the nest peace can be put better: we should decide to make the world safe for small nations.
That phrase implies all that is essential. If the world is safe for small nations, it will be safe for all nations. If the world is safe for small nations, it will be an ordered world in which the rights of each nation are determined by justice and not by relative strength, as in an ordered community the unarmed citizen is safe beneath the protection of the law. If the world is safe for small nations, it will be a world in which the human spirit can blossom in all its infinite variety of national cultures and not be beaten flat into a totalitarian mould.
How can^ the world be made safe for small nations? Not by their dependence on a larger neighbour, for that destroys nationhood. Not by their own arms and not by grouping themselves with other small nations; not even the largest single nation in the world to-day can be safe by its own arms, for safety does not mean living always on the brink of war, even if one survives war. It means security

being without the fact or the constant fear of war. Security for all nations, small and great, can come only through the enthronement of impartial justice between nations and the arming of justice with decisive force for her decrees. "The scales of justice", as Mr. Winston Churchill once said, "are vain without her swcrd". Who is to supply international justice with her sword and wield it for her?
The Prime Minister ten days ago said that Canada was a world power. While Canada is still a small power in terms of military strength and population she is great in resources, enormously great in possibilities. If the hon. member for Vancouver South by his interpolation meant that those possibilities were practically unlimited, then I agree with him completely. But the one basis on which we can grow steadily toward a greater maturity, a greater strength and a greater usefulness to the world, is that we should have conceptions of our country which can be shared by all Canadians, and not just Canadians of Anglo-Saxon descent or of French descent, or other descent, but Canadians of all descents. It should be remembered that some of them cannot have the same views of our country's relationships as some of us have. We should not go to any extreme of views in one direction or the other. In the middle there is an idea of Canada as a free, independent, autonomous nation, associated with the British commonwealth and with our neighbour, the United States, with whom we have closer relations than have ever existed between any other two nations before, a Canada willing, in [Mr. Claxton.l
fact desirous of playing its full part in the affairs of the world, because there is our interest and because our interest is not in any way separated from the interests of any other nation. We have no axe to grind, nothing to gain except security and peace for ourselves and our people; but as we gain security and peace for our people we can contribute to the security and peace of other people. Any conceptions that my hon. friends opposite have of the British commonwealth or any other association must be big enough to conceive of the world gradually growing into a community, because that is what it is becoming, and the sooner we shape our ideas and our ideals and our hopes to that conception, the better it will be for ourselves and for our people.

speechtext:
I will answer it right away. My hon. friend asked the following question on July 9:
Will the Prime Minister make a general statement or table the agreement between Canada and the United States covering the position of the latter as to its use of or interest in the Alaska highway after the war?
The answer to that is that the exchange of notes on the Alaska highway, tabled in the House of Commons on March 18, 1942, provided that:
At the conclusion of the war that part of the highway which lies in Canada' shall become in all respects an integral part of the Canadian highway system, subject to the understanding that there shall at no time be imposed any discriminatory conditions in relation to the use of the road as between Canadian and United States civilian traffic.
Then, second, my hon. friend asked:
Will the Prime Minister make a similar statement or table the agreement as to the ownership, the interest in and use of the pipeline from the Fort Norman oil fields to the refinery at Whitehorse and in the refinery; the amount of money involved in the construction of the pipeline and the oil refinery?

Supply-External Affairs
The answer is:
Under the terms of an agreement between the Canadian and United States governments, the complete test of which cannot yet be made public for security reasons, the United States is paying the costs of the project and the Canadian government is providing sites for structures and rights of way essential to the project, and is also making oil rights available under proper regulations. The Canadian government has also agreed during the war to facilitate the entry into Canada of equipment, labour and personnel for construction and maintenance of the project, and to waive import duties, taxes, licence fees, et cetera. Royalties on oil produced under this project are also waived for the duration of the war. The United States government retains ownership of the pipeline and refinery until the end of the war. at which time they will be offered for sale, with the Canadian government being given prior right of purchase. Failing a satisfactory sale being made, the disposition of the pipeline and refinery will be referred to the Permanent Joint Board on Defence. It is impossible at this time to estimate the amount of money involved in the construction of the pipeline and refinery.
Then my hon. friend asked:
Will title to the land through which the pipeline runs be alienated to the United States or to any company, or will it remain the property of Canada?
The answer is:
Title to the land through which the pipeline runs remains in the crown in the right of Canada.
The last question was:
Will individuals or companies other than Imperial Oil have the use of the pipeline after the war?
The answer is:
Under the agreement between the two governments, the pipeline and refinery will be offered for sale at the conclusion of the war at a valuation set by two appraisers, one named by Canada and one by the United States. The Canadian government will be given the first option to purchase. If the option is not exercised within three months, the facilities may be offered for sale by public tender with the amount of the valuation as the reserve price.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: PROPOSALS WITH RESPECT TO DELIVERIES FROM DEALERS TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
It has already been emphasized
that this is a very important debate. The number of subjects within the purview of the Department of External Affairs is quite extensive, and all of them are exceedingly important. Other members of this group are dealing with some of the other subjects.
I wish to confine my remarks to just one subject and, in fact, to one particular phase of that subject; I refer to the problems arising out of the refugee situation, and in particular to the terrible plight of the people of the Jewish race.
There are times, Mr. Chairman, when members of this house rise to speak because we know we are dealing with matters in which there is wide and keen public interest. I think it is only realism, as hon. members will recognize, to say quite frankly that this is a subject in which there can hardly be said to be wide public interest; rather it is a subject in which, I feel, a lead should be given to our people.
I rise to speak on this matter primarily because of humanitarian instincts which, I am sure, are shared by practically all hon. members, instincts which prompt many of us to raise our voices whenever the opportunity is afforded on behalf of people suffering untold persecution.
I should like to set the tone of my remarks and perhaps give expression to my attitude on this question by reading a few sentences from the printed copy of a broadcast given over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation network last Easter Sunday by Watson Thomson:
Retribution towards the nazi criminals is certainly not enough: any pagan, any nazi storm trooper can do that thing. Upon us is a higher and a harder obligation. Not to pity the Jews, not to sentimentalize over them, not to pass resolutions about them. But to rise up and act with all the passion of an awakened human conscience, and save Jewish lives. Save them- not to send them to Eritrea or Madagascar, but to live with them ourselves, learning to say what we like and what we dislike about them as those may who desire understanding and reconciliation, learning to listen to what they have in ancient grievance against us; so that the past may be eaten up into a tolerant present and carried forward into a creative future of living together.
It might tend to shorten my remarks if I were to give a few quotations which summarize the situation with respect to Jewish
Supply-External Affairs

refugees. I should like to read a bit from a pamphlet entitled "Let My People Go," written by Victor Gollancz:
Of the 6,000,000 Jews or so who were living at the outbreak of the war in what is at present nazi-oocupied Europe, a high proportion-say between one and two million-have been deliberately murdered by the nazis and their satellites.
No discrimination has been made in favour of pregnant women, babies, children, the sick, the very old. On the contrary, discrimination, such as it is, has been in favour of men from whom an adequate last ounce can be got in German war factories.
The murders are taking the form of random shootings, mass shootings, mass electrocutions, mass poison-gassing, and transportation in conditions which inevitably involve death during the journey. This is over and above slow starvation by the allotment of hopelessly inadequate rations, or no rations at all. . . .
This policy, which has been pursued since the outbreak of the war, has been greatly speeded up during the last few months. Unless something effective is done within a very few months these six million Jews will all be dead except fifty thousand or so in the countries at present neutral and perhaps a few tens of thousands whom Hitler may find it convenient to work to the last ounce of their strength in his own war factories.
I turn now to a sentence in the broadcast given by Watson Thomson- on Easter Sunday. It is very brief, but it tells a great deal about the horrible plight of these people:
The armed guards surrounding the ghetto walls have a standard rate now of one hundred zlotys for which price they will consent to give a Jew the privilege of being shot at his own request.
I should like to call the attention of hon. members to another document which I think it would be well for everyone to read. It appears under the heading, "Starvation Over Europe." Its sub-title is, "Made in Germany." The book has been published by the Institute of Jewish Affairs, and I find in the back of it eight or ten pages of citations giving the authority for the material contained in it. The material has been collected from William Beveridge, the London Economist, the London Economic Journal, "World Economic Survey" of the League of Nations, Foreign Affairs, New York Times, New York Herald-Tribune, London Times, "Survey of Central and Eastern Europe" published by the League of Nations, "Central European Observer" published in London, and a whole host of credible documents and newspapers from all parts of the world.
This book sets out the stark fact that the nazis are making terrible use of the lessons of science with particular reference to feeding. It is pointed out that it is part of 'the German plan so to allot and apportion food among the peoples of occupied Europe that the strongest
Mr. Knowles.]
will be of course the Germans, both in Germany itself and in olher -parts of Europe; the next strongest physically will be those from whom the Germans can get work in their war factories; and so on down -the list of various races and nationalities under the control of the nazis at the present time.
I read that Hitler's scientists not only made a careful study of what had happened in Germany during the last war. They closely calculated the subtle distinctions between minimum protective diet, malnutrition produced by specific deficiencies, slow starvation caused by denial of cell-replenishing foods, and finally actual famine. Their research also taught them that over a long period certain deficiencies spell disaster in the form of national debilitation and a stunted generation. Accordingly on the basis of this knowledge and research the Germans are doing two things. On the one hand, they are seeing -to it that their own people are well fed, scientifically fed, so that they will be strong for the conflict in which they are engaged, and also for another eventuality to which I will refer in a moment. On the other hand, they are making use of the scientific knowledge which they have gained to see to it that the peoples whom they conquer are strong enough only to serve German ends, and as far as certain nationalities and races are concerned, particularly the Jews, that they pass out of the picture altogether.
I said there was another eventuality to which I would call attention, and perhaps I can do it best by quoting directly from the book:
In their ruthless logic the nazi leaders have not ignored the possibility of ultimate defeat. Should Germany be destined to fail again on the battlefield they are determined that their system of feeding and starving, as applied during the war years, shall result in a radical and permanent shift in the demographic balance of power.
The Germans, in other words, realize that they can lose and may lose this war. They are determined that if they lose it, when it is all over, their people will be physically so much stronger than the peoples of other parts of Europe that, as it were, in starting from scratch on the continent of Europe, they will have a better chance in the scramble that will ensue.
Just in passing, I should point to the lessons that are to be drawn from that situation. They tell us, of course, that we should be making the fullest use of the scientific knowledge we have to make sure that in so far as it is possible, with the foods at our command, we should have a strong people both for the war and for the post-war period. They remind

us, too, of the problem that will face us when the war is over-the problem of feeding millions of people on the continent of Europe. It will be a case not only of getting to them so .much bulk, as far as food is concerned, but of getting to them the right kind of food, which they are now denied, in order that they may rebuild a race whose physical condition will be seriously deteriorated. That, of course, has very wide implications for us in view of our situation as a largely agricultural country. May I give to the committee some of the statistics which have been compiled in this book. The material is set out in tables which are quite interesting, though they are certainly alarming.
