Rather we should consider the facts and figures such as I have given, and as human beings see if we cannot come to a decision as to what we are to do. I should like to refer hon. members to a memorandum submitted to the Bermuda refugee conference by the world Jewish congress. In the beginning of this memorandum reference is made to the conditions I have just placed before the committee and it goes on to say:
The nazis have never concealed their determination to destroy European Jewry. As late as March 14, 1943, Doctor Goebhels, in an interview given to foreign press .representatives, declared: "Germany is firmly convinced that the Jews are an international disease which must be exterminated in Europe."
Then on February 19, Doctor Goebbels made this further comment:
"If hostile foreign countries raise a sanctimonious protest against our anti-Semitic policy and shed hypocritical crocodile tears over our measures against Jewry, that cannot prevent us from doing what is necessary. The warnings of retribution uttered repeatedly by the most authoritative spokesmen of the democratic world have had no deterrent effect on the enemy. There remain only two ways in which the total destruction of the Jewish population on the continent of Europe can be prevented: 1. The sending of supplies under proper safeguards to places of detention and remnants of Jewish communities which survive; and 2. To remove as many Jews as possible from nazi-oontrolled areas to places of refuge.

If the gravity of the problem is not recognized, and action not taken immediately, the

I was glad to note, in the Prime Minister's statement this morning that he had something to say about refugees, and that he dealt specifically with the problems facing the Jewish people. News has just been received that of 2,000 children, from two years of age upwards, deported from Vichy France in cattle trucks, half were dead on arrival at their destination and the rest were dying.
The point is, Mr. Chairman, that waiting to help these people in the best way that we can later on is, in the opinion of some of us. 
really not good enough in view of the fact that many of them-thousands, perhaps millions-will not be there to help. Many of them we could not help, no matter how much initiative the government or the people of this country might display. I intimated when I rose in my place that I realized this is not a subject of wide popular interest to the people of this country. After all, Jews are only a very small portion of our population. They are also human in the sense that they deserve humane treatment. I remind hon. members that they are part of the human race and have contributed to the race some of the greatest characters in our history. The culture that they have given to us, particularly of a religious nature, is something that our civilization would be a great deal poorer without. I believe it would increase our own sense of humanity, and increase our own consciousness of the fact that we are trying to establish a better world in which we will get rid of racial hatred, prejudice and antagonism. I dare to hope that the government, fully conscious of the attitude of many people toward this question, might seek in this instance not to do just what they are being asked to do by some small sections of the population, but to give a lead in this matter.

Mr. Chairman, by the look of some of the hon. members this evening it would appear that this subject is not a particularly popular one, and yet I consider it necessary to make a few remarks in support of what has been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I am in agreement wth him that perhaps not quite as wide a section of our people are interested in this subject as should be. Yet I believe there is enough public sympathy and there are enough people in this country who are wondering why Canada is not able to take a greater lead among the united nations in helping the refugees from Europe to ensure sufficient interest in this matter to make it worth while. One unfortunate aspect of this whole problem is that the fascist propaganda has permeated farther than the nations under fascist control. If we do have to have in our own so-called democratic country a certain amount of anti-Semitic feeling, it is the product of fascist ideology and should have no place in any democratic country. The persecution of any minority people becomes, later, an obsession and madness. Intolerance is just a barbaric custom; it is a form more or less of a persecution mania which we thought we had left behind us long ago in the middle ages. To accept any form of intolerance is to debase ourselves to Hitler's level of intelligence and barbarity. I should like to quote from a book published in 1937, one which has been very widely read, and which has been acknowledged to be one of the finest statements prepared on the subject of the fascist state. It was written by Professor Brady, associate professor of economics of the university of California. He calls his book "The Spirit and Structure of German Fascism", and he quotes from a statement by Darre, reichminister of agriculture, in which he says:
The Semites reject everything that pertains to the pig. The Nordic peoples, on the contrary, accord the pig the highest possible honour ... in the cult of the'Germans the pig occupies the first place and is the first among the domestic animals ... This predominance of the pig, the sacred animal destined to sacrifices among the Nordic peoples, has drawn its
Supply-External Affairs

originality from the great trees of the German forest ... Thus out of the darkness of earliest history arise two human races whose attitude in respect of pigs presents an absolute contrast ... The Semites and the pig are faunal and thus physiological opposites. It is not unthinkable that the eating of pig flesh by the Semite sets up physiological disharmonies in his body ... The Semites do not understand the pig, they do not accept the pig, they reject the pig, whereas this animal occupies the first place in the cult of the Nordic peoples.
This is only one small illustration of the wholesale absurdity upon which fascist theories have been built, theories which to-day are responsible for the ghastly slaughter of millions of most innocent people. It is perhaps more necessary that we should understand why the German nazis used antiSemitism as a weapon in their hands. I shall continue to quote from the same chapter by Professor Brady. He says:
By outlawing Jews it provides a partial solution for the job hunger of loyal nazi party adherents. The bulk of these active rank and file adherents fall into the middle strata of professional and trades people on the one hand, and politically active youth in search for jobs in these fields on the other. It is in precisely these fields that the Jews, comprising less than one-half of one per cent of the total population, were the most active.
He goes on to say:
The Jews served very well as ''bogeyman" for the nazi strategists. The German peasant is led to believe that the Jew stole all his hard-won earnings away from him by some devil's magic on the commodity exchanges. The petit-bourgeois classes were told that the Jew aspired to control all professional jobs, ruin small tradesmen (note the campaigns against Wertheims and other large departmental stores), and dominate for "racial purposes" all big industry and the _ financial machinery of the country. Labour is asked to believe that cynical and self-seeking Jews, under the guise of Marxism, stirred up labour discontent which they could exploit to their own cruel advantage and in which they did, as a matter of course, continuously betray the interests they affected to represent. Young girls and women are taught that physical contact with the Jew will corrupt them biologically.
By these means the "attention of the masses was diverted" to see the Jew as the cause of low farm prices, high retail prices, adulteration of goods, onerous tax burdens for reparations payments, low wages, unsatisfactory labour conditions, and many other crimes against the Aryan people. . . . Needless to say, not only did the Jews not "control" or set interest rates, agricultural indebtedness, or speculative activity, but also the nazis did not abolish these activities. What they attempted to do was to lead the populace to believe that in suppressing the Jews, they had corrected the abuses of which so many had with such justice so long and bitterly complained.
There is without doubt a widespread feeling among large sections of the British people that more could be done to prevent loss of
fMrs. Nielsen.]
life at the present time. Reference has already been made to the pamphlet published by Victor Gollancz entitled) "Let My People Go". It is a significant fact that over 150,000 copies of this small pamphlet have been bought by the British people since the beginning of this year. Some of our greatest world figures have expressed horror at the continued barbarity toward the Jewish people, notably the Pope, the President of .the United States, Mr. Churchill and also our own Prime Minister. We are told by some that of course the solution is to win the war. Naturally I agree with that. One cannot quarrel with the truth, of that statement. But the point is that while the united nations are straining every nerve and effort to do .that, how many hundreds of thousands of these people are to be left to their horrible fate until the war is won. Cannot something more be done to prevent the slaughter of these people, before we are in a position to establish control over Europe? I would remind hon. members of the committee that sympathy for these people, alone, will not save their lives.
On December 17 last year a statement was made in the British House of Commons on this problem by Mr. Anthony Eden. He said at that time that those who were responsible for these crimes will receive retribution. But retribution in a year or two years' time will not save the lives of those who to-night, at this very moment, may be meeting a fate more tragic than either you or I could conceive, and they are meeting that fate at the hands of these demented sadists.
These horrors are so far away from us they have not touched us intimately as a nation. I should like .to quote from this pamphlet written by Mr. Victor Gollancz, who is himself a Jew. I do not wish to add any horror, any more than anyone else does; and yet, as I said before, these things are so far away from us that I believe if we could only bring them near to us, and try to feel ourselves as these Jewish people and other refugees on the continent are feeling at this very moment, it might help perhaps to instill into us the necessity for doing something.
I quote this from page 8 of his pamphlet:
You will read that ten thousand are being sent every day from Warsaw to the slaughter camps further east: you will read that one hundred and fifty men. women and children are being packed into a sealed coach just big enough to hold forty, so that when they arrive the living, the dying, and the dead fall out together, and the peasants fly from the stench. Forget "ten thousand": forget "one hundred and fifty"; or rather, remember them only for purposes of multiplication, and in order to grasp the magnitude of the horror. For a few brief moments, be just one of those human beings, whose body,

with its nerves that can suffer so, and whose mind and soul, with all their resources of terror and despair, are concealed by the cold abstraction of "one hundred and fifty" and "ten thousand" and "six million". And then be another, and another. Be the mother flinging her baby from a sixth-storey window: be a girl of nine, torn from her parents and standing in the dark of a moving truck with two corpses pressed close against her; be an old Jew at the door of the electrocution chamber. And only then when you have been each of these for a few short moments, do the multiplication.
I would say that this is definitely not a Jewish problem. It is a problem of humanity itself. After the matter had been discussed in the British House of Commons by Mr. Anthony Eden, one of the members of the house, Miss Rathbone, wrote a letter to the News Chronicle of December 16, in which she said this:
Few people realize the rigidity of the regulations by which the home secretary now controls the entry of refugees to this country and the corresponding regulations affecting the colonies. Except for allied nationals specially asked for by their governments and a few children who cannot in effect be brought here, the door is practically barred. . . . The first step, therefore, is to demand the revision of these regulations, so that refugees for whom the only chance of escape from torture and death is a visa for a safe country shall no longer be met at every turn by the notice "you may not enter here . The whole matter has larger implications. The settlement during and after the war of refugees, especially the Jews, concerns not only the home office, but also the foreign office, the dominions and the colonies.
At least it seems that at the present time, through the good offices of some of the neutral countries, we might approach the fascist nations. I remember this morning the Prime Minister said that we can have no faith in them. I agree with him. Of course Hitler can either accept or refuse. Naturally there is the danger that he may use the method of infiltration, by sending his spies in among the refugees. Naturally the greatest care will have to be taken. It would seem to me that if we made some approach to the neutral nations it would give some comfort at least to the people in the occupied countries and even those in Germany who have still some spark of decency within them and realize the disastrous fate that is before the Jewish people and others. Surely adult refugees could be placed in concentration camps so that, with the very greatest care having to be exercised, not one of [DOT]them could go outside for any purpose, and therefore the danger of spies to a very great degree would be controlled. In parts of Africa and Palestine it would appear that there must be room for refugee people. At present small numbers of refugee people are getting through to neutral countries, but the trouble is that the neutral countries are so
small and are so overburdened with refugees that it is impossible for them to be continually taking more. Therefore they are forced to shut the door to further refugees. But if we were able to remove from some of the neutral countries the refugees who are already there and place them in camps in Africa or Palestine, it would make room for more of these unfortunates to come through to the neutral countries, and surely if it were only for the sake of a handful of refugees it would be worth the attempt. I quote further from Mr. Gollancz, on the question of allowing refugees into Palestine:
Palestine could absorb 50,000 Jews in its war industries immediately, to the great benefit of the allied war effort. There would also be room for thousands of children. The country and the allied war machinery are, indeed, crying out for more men. The military authorities need 30,000 unskilled and 5,000 skilled workers. Agricultural production in Palestine is gravely curtailed for lack of labour.
He continues:
In view of all this, what possible reason can there be, in common sense or humanity, for the present policy? What is that policy?
In the government White Paper of May, 1939, it was laid down that during the five years beginning April, 1939, 75,000 Jewish immigrants should be admitted into the country, and that thereafter Jewish immigration should cease permanently. This is not the place to discuss whether this restriction was compatible with the terms of the Balfour declaration, which declared the intention of setting up a Jewish national home in Palestine, or with the terms of the mandate based on it. Those who read the White Paper will perhaps feel in the very uneasiness of its phraseology the confession that, "for political reasons", a trust was being broken.	_
However that may be, 75.000 by April, 1944, was the number to be admitted. The number so far admitted is less than 40,000. That is to say, according to the terms of the White Paper itself, more than 35,000 immigration certificates are still outstanding during the next fifteen months. Is it conceivable that the government can refuse to grant them now, more especially in view of the economic needs of the country which have been mentioned above? Apparently it is conceivable. But if the refusal is persisted in, then the government cannot be held blameless for the fate of men, women and children who might otherwise have been saved.
It will not help any mother or any parent of a child in an occupied country to know that the murderer of the child will be punished at some future time. But we can try to save that child now, and if we fail to do so I think you and I might just as well acknowledge that the story of the Good Samaritan has fallen on deaf ears, that we have failed to apply that principle to the need which has arisen in our own day and age, and that like other nations we are passing by on the other side of the road and not heeding the cries of those who need our assistance.

We are fighting to-day the greatest robber and the greatest murderer of mankind that the world has ever known, and if you and I have a conscience we have to see that the necessary ways and means are found, even though a certain degree of secrecy will have to be maintained; for, of course, we must see that Hitler does not use anything we may do to further his own aims or help him in any way. I quote again from Mr. Gollancz' publication. He says that on December 27, Reynolds newspaper:
. . . publishes details of a manifesto issued by a conference of all anti-fascist groups in Germany, which recently met secretly, and which declares that peace will be possible only after complete destruction of the Hitler regime, that all concentration camps must be closed, that all anti-Jewish and race laws must be annulled, that religious, economic, political and press freedom must be reestablished, and that there must be a foreign policy based on peace and international cooperation. The manifesto is being broadcast by the secret German Freedom Radio, at the risk of death or torture for everyone involved, and is being directed to the German army as well as to the home front.
We must not neglect to realize that there are some people in Germany who would help if only we would let them know across the distances of the world that we were endeavouring to do something. I cannot help feeling that there is need for Canada asking Britain for a revision of the regulations regarding the entry of refugees. If we were to help the neutral countries to evacuate the refugees who are already there to parts of Africa and Palestine, it would be possible for more refugees to go into the neutral countries from the occupied countries of Europe. I believe that this country could collect money for the necessary camps, food, ships, transportation facilities and so on for this service. Broadcasts could go out from this country and fiom other countries, and the Catholic people of this country should ask the Vatican to send out broadcasts, because they would possibly be listened to by more people in the occupied countries than broadcasts coming from our own or from the British government. In that way we could feel that we had at least tried to do something for these unfortunate people, and we would have the satisfaction of knowing we had done our best for these 
people-not Jews, nor Czechs nor Poles-just people, remembering that what was said long ago still holds:
Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.

Mr. Chairman, we have listened to various subjects discussed to-day. I rise more particularly	to draw to	the	attention	of	thePrime Minister and of the committee a subject of vital interest to the people of Canada, although	perhaps of	more interest	to	the
people of the Pacific coast.
I wish to draw to the Prime Minister's attention,	a matter which	might affect	ourfisheries,	particularly	the	fisheries	of	the
Pacific coast. The matter I have in mind has to do with the waters off our Canadian shores and beyond the three-mile limit.
Dealing with our salmon fisheries, may I say to the members of the committee that all the salmon caught off the Pacific coast of British Columbia and in our rivers are born and reared in Canadian waters, streams and creeks. After a period there of from one to two years they go out to sea and return, according to the variety of the salmon, in either three or four years, with some varieties staying out until they are almost five years old. Then they return from the open sea and head inward to the Eraser river and other Canadian rivers.
During the time they are at sea these fish feed and grow on what is known as the continental shelf, which is a ridge rising from the bed of the ocean to within two or three hundred feet of the surface. This ridge or continental shelf runs parallel to our entire coast-line at a distance of some twenty miles off shore. It is along these banks that the salmon feed until the time comes for them to leturn to the place where they were born for the purpose of spawning, after which they die.
I urge upon the Prime Minister that these waters should be recognized as Canadian or United States waters for the protection of our salmon and for fishing purposes. Vessels from any country could come along and wipe out our entire salmon fishing industry by fishing the continental shelf. The United States and Canada have entered into a treaty to rehabilitate and preserve the sockeye salmon fishing. At the last meeting of the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries commission a resolution was passed which I should like to place on^ the records of the house, because the matter is of vital concern not only to the

Supply-External Affairs
people of the Pacific coast but to all our people as well. The resolution reads as
follows:
Whereas, the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries Commission was created pursuant to a convention entered into between the United States and the Dominion of Canada primarily for the purpose of rehabilitating the Fraser river sockeye salmon supply, and
Whereas, it is confidently expected by the commission that its projected work in the removal of obstructions and in the regulation of the fishery will be successful, and
Whereas, said convention included within its terms the territorial waters and the high seas westward from the Dominion of Canada and the United States of America within lines therein described, and
Whereas, it seems probable that it will be practical for fishermen and vessels of other nations to operate on Swiftsure banks and other places more than three miles off shore and if permitted to do so in disregard of the regulations adopted by the commission, may drastically interfere with the restoration of the salmon supply referred to.
Now, therefore, be it resolved that the attention of the governments of the two nations be called to this situation in order that such steps may be taken as, in the opinion of said governments, may appear advisable.
It is most important now, I believe, that steps be taken by both the United States and Canada in this matter, and I would ask that the Prime Minister's office start negotiations with the United States along the lines outlined in the resolution.
I would draw to the attention of the committee that the terms of the treaty concerning sockeye salmon fisheries which was concluded between the United States and Canada specify very vaguely the extent of our jurisdiction over the offshore waters, because article 1 of the treaty provides that it shall apply to the following waters:
The territorial waters and the high seas westward from the western coast of the United States of America and the Dominion of Canada.
I maintain that the limits set should be more specific and definite; as the treaty stands, these waters would extend right out to the shores of Japan. What we are asking is that we go at least as far as the continental shelf where the sockeye salmon feed for three or four years before returning to Canadian waters.
There is another matter along similar lines that I should like also at this time to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister and to the members of the committee. This has to do with the waters lying between Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland of British Columbia, and known as Hecate strait.
Queen Charlotte islands are a large group of islands extending 100 miles in length and have an area of 4,005 square miles, in size about twice the size of Prince Edward Island.
The territory equals over 20 million acres of land. The narrowest width of sea is at the north end, which is only some nineteen miles from the mainland, whereas at the south end it is some fifty miles wide.
The waters between the islands and the mainland are known as Hecate strait, and at the present time these waters are fished by both Canadian and United States fishermen.
Since Canada has not designated these waters as "Canadian waters", there is nothing, however, to prevent fishing vessels from any foreign nation from fishing within the strait itself.
I wish to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister that Canada did take some steps some years ago. As long ago as 1896 Canadian patrol vessels warned foreign fishermen against operating in these waters. Captain Walbran of the D.G.S. Quadra reported that in that year he had warned United States vessels they were fishing in Canadian waters, and that these, after having been warned, left the strait.
There are many instances in the world today where certain countries claim' territorial rights extending considerable distances over large expanses of water, and it may interest hon. members to know that the so-called three-mile limit, which is usually referred to as the limit which a country should have in the exercise of its rights, differs entirely throughout the world. In fact, there is no such thing as an international law on the matter. Some countries, like Russia, established a twelve-mile limit. The Bering sea tribunal in 1893 established a sixty-mile zone for fur-seals. Delaware bay, which is twenty miles wide, is recognized as within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States, while Chesapeake bay, which is twelve miles wide at the entrance and extends 270 miles long, is entirely closed to all foreign fishermen. Hudson bay is another example. Canada prohibited any fishing in Hudson bay for anyone without a licence from the dominion.
Great Britain, which has throughout .long years fought for the freedom of the seas, itself prosecuted a Captain Mortensen, who was operating a Norwegian steam trawler called Niobe, which vessel was seized for fishing in Moray firth. Captain Mortensen was fined for fishing five miles from shore.
Uruguay exercises control over one-half of the river La Plata, though the river at its mouth is 135 miles wide and is fifty miles wide 100 miles from the open sea.
Going back to ancient history-this may interest hon. members who may believe in the universality of the so-called three-mile limit -Venice once claimed and enforced the entire Adriatic sea, which was 500 miles long by
Supply- External Affairs

100 miles wide. Every ship entering there was searched; even the Pope of that day protested about his ships being molested.
The first definition of the three-mile limit occurred in 1818 when a treaty between Great Britain and United States was signed, but it is interesting to note that neither of these nations has fully adhered to this. Even the mile has differed over a period of time. The mile in Queen Elizabeth's time was 5,000 feet; in the 38th year of her reign it was 5,240 feet. The Spanish mile is 4,656 yards; the Dutch, 8,240 yards; the French, 4,263 yards; the German short mile, 6,859 yards. Therefore, when one speaks of the three-mile limit, what does that actually mean; which mile are they speaking of, the English land mile, which is 5,280 feet, or the nautical mile, 6,075 feet, or do they refer to the French, Dutch or that of the Spaniard?
Here we have, Mr. Chairman, large islands lying off the Pacific coast, and no steps yet have been taken to preserve for fishing the waters lying between them. It is my opinion that steps should be taken now to declare that the waters lying off our shores and between Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland, known as the Hecate strait, be known as Canadian waters, and I am appealing to the Prime Minister now that the matters that I have spoken of be taken seriously and that steps be taken to discuss this situation both with the United States and with our own Canadian departments.
May I point out that this is an opportune time for making an approach to the United States in the matter. It may interest hon. members to know that the United States and Canada are the only two countries in the world which have treaties with regard to fish. The treaty they put into effect to protect the fur-seals has increased the fur-seal herd' from 100,000 to a flock of upwards of 2,000,000 and brought a net revenue to this country of $312,000 last year. Our halibut might have disappeared entirely by now if the United States and Canada had not entered into a treaty to protect and rehabilitate the halibut, which is fished for off the Canadian and Alaskan shores.
Coming to the recent salmon treaty signed by the United States and Canada to rehabilitate the sockeye salmon, I might point out that at one time the catch in the Fraser river waters amounted to two and a half million cases, whereas last year, which was quite a high yield year, some 600,000 cases only were canned by our fishermen.
There will be a great demand for food after the war. There will also be a great demand

for fish. No steps have been taken to exclude from fishing off our shores fishing vessels of other nationals.
In 1938, at a conference on the Pacific coast of representatives from various north and south American countries, as well as representatives from Japan, it was pointed out to the delegates that the halibut was protected and had been increasing as a result of the treaty and that the salmon was also protected and was not allowed to be entirely destroyed, but the Japanese delegates at that conference said to the gathering, "We have caught salmon and other varieties of fish off your shores, but we never noticed either the union jack or the stars and stripes on their backs." In other words, they took the view that fish in the open seas belong to any national or any person who goes after them and catches them. We take a different attitude, especially as they are born in our waters. We say that owing to our protection and the treaty between the two countries, both halibut and salmon have been increasing, and we argue that they would probably have disappeared in some of the fishing banks had the two countries not entered1 into such a treaty. In fact, we have led the world in the matter of fishery treaties.
I am strongly of opinion that steps should be taken now with regard to the waters off our shores in the Hecate strait as well as the strait of Juan de Fuca, where our salmon feed on the continental banks.	[DOT]

I do not propose to make my remarks of any length to-night, but I would refer to certain statements made this morning in committee. I have here a cutting from to-day's Ottawa Journal in which I am charged with hating the Jews. I will not read the whole thing, but this is not the first time that my name has been bandied about the country and has appeared in the press as a Jew-baiter by some, and a Jew-hater by others. It seems to be taken for granted that merely to criticize, in fact merely to mention a Jew, is to lay oneself open to the charge of being a Jew-baiter, and coming from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, as it did this morning, I think that only

Supply-External Affairs
adds to the offence. Surely if there is a group in this house the members of which are wont to express their hatred for this person or that person, whenever they rise in their places, it is the group-not all of them, but some of the group-of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, as I believe the Minister of Finance remarked the other night. Apparently anybody who manages to make more than an average success of his affairs is attacked, or at least is regarded with hatred by some of the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group.
On another occasion I was speaking on the budget, and I read a list of the leading international financiers whose names were all household words. I merely read the list. Everybody knows them, and I merely asked, how many are British names, how many French names, and for that matter how many Christian? At once I was assailed. In fact, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) immediately rose to his feet and said, "No Jew baiting." That got out into the press. Later on, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation was speaking in the house and he referred to my criticism of the address that Mr. Sandwell gave some months ago on the League of Nations, in which he advocated that the Canadian people should surrender their loyalty to the crown and hand it over to international control.
I have here a copy of an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press. It says:
Mr. Jaques raised the question of whether the views of B. K. Sandwell, the Toronto editor, on a supranational world order were seditious. When M. J. Coldwell, the C.C.F. leader, who is a member of the League of Nations Society, sought to reply, Mr. Jaques interrupted by muttering, "Jewish bankers", and "gold standard." Mr. Coldwell said, "I am afraid my hon. friend has the gold standard on his brain."
I will challenge anybody in this house to find those words on Hansard. I never said that.

More than that, Mr. Chairman, I am perfectly willing to stand on my reputation in this house and out of the house, too, as a loyal citizen of Canada, and' I will challenge anybody in this house or out of
it to finds one authentic quotation of mine in which I have showed in any way that I am either a Jew-baiter or in favour of Jew persecution. I will say more. I happen to be one of the few members of this house who, in September, 1939, demanded, in the name of this group, that Canada should wage total war against the German nazi gangsters. I could quote those views if necessary, but I think that is remembered by those who were present in the house.	As the Montreal
Gazette in an editorial recently said, the Social Credit group was the only group in the house at that time who stood and demanded total war against the nazi gangsters. I am not saying, "I told you so." I am not making the statement in that sense; I am merely saying that actions speak louder than words. What was the attitude of those members, and especially the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation who is now such a champion of the persecuted Jews? I quote from Hansard of September 9, 1939, at page 55 as follows:
Canada should be prepared to defend her own shores, but her assistance overseas should be limited to economic aid and must not include conscription of man-power or the sending of any expeditionary force.
I do not wish to rub that in at all; I am merely stating it. Perhaps I had better address it to the Jews and ask them who are their best friends. Suppose Britain had received no aid and had gone down, as she was within an ace of doing. The result might have been that Hitler would have controlled the western hemisphere as well as the eastern hemisphere, and the granting of aid to all persecuted minorities would have been impossible.
The cause of the little flare-up this morning was a remark I made which was not heard by Hansard. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was speaking as usual in a sort of global way, although I have never accepted his global authority. My own private opinion is that it is "globaloney", but when he claimed that his memory goes back two thousand years I found that a little too much to swallow. The hon. gentleman told the old story or fable if you like, about Joseph and the Jewish refugees going into Egypt and becoming the parents of the founder of our Christian religion. I merely said that the only thing wrong with that story was that he was not a Jew. My authority for saying that is the Dean of St. Paul's, who, I take it, is an eminent authority on the subject. I do not profess to be an authority at all.
Supply-External Affairs

Those who are so solicitous at the present time for the fortunes of the Jews in Europe are precisely those who opposed any preparation or rearmament against the growing threat of Hitler. I make that statement without fear of challenge. All minorities, including Jews, have enjoyed greater protection and justice and have received fairer treatment under British rule, under British crown, or even, if you like, under British imperialism than under any other control. I say that without fear of contradiction. But it is precisely those people who profess such sympathy for these wretched, persecuted minorities who are working and have been working tooth and nail to destroy that very British protection. That is the stand I take.
I think I can say for the party to which I belong, for that matter for the whole Social Credit movement throughout the British empire, that we anchor ourselves absolutely to the British crown. We believe that that is the best guarantee of peace and justice for the minorities and, if you like, for the majorities as well. We are utterly opposed1 to any scheme or any proposal or any plan that would surrender any part of that control to any international organization for any reason whatever. We believe in cooperation as there has been cooperation for the last hundred years with our neighbour to the south. Why interfere with relations which have been so peaceful and pleasant in the past?
I think most hon. members will realize that I am not likely to rise and talk merely for the sake of talking. I am talking tonight because I feel it is my duty to do so. I think that is realized by every hon. member. And I say to those outside the -house that although the flesh may be weak, I can assure them that, the spirit is as strong as ever. I realize the charges that will be made in the press after this morning to the effect that I am a Jew-baiter or a Jew-hater. Let me say that since the session of two years ago I have faced the grim reaper, not for a few minutes but for many months. As I lay in the hospital I thought deeply and long. I do not think I need to assure hon. members that I have no axe to grind. I have no ambitions in this world other than to establish the truth as I see it and to make conditions better for those who follow me. As I say, I have no ambitions, and, if I had, they would be out of the question, of ever leading a party or planning the order of this country, let alone of the universe. That is not for me. Perhaps I have an advantage to make up for that. I have no fear of any

individual or any group of individuals. Why should I have? I have nothing to lose. The idea which is prevalent and which seems to be growing that the Jews are above criticism, or that to criticize a Jew or even to mention the fact that anybody is a Jew is to lay oneself open to the charge of Jew baitiDg is preposterous nonsense, and I do not propose to take the slightest notice of it. I am not afraid of any man whether he has a hooked nose or a forked tail. Why should I be? Immediately the Jew is criticized, somebody takes the attitude that nobody has any right to do it and, if he does it, he is indulging in sacrilege. That is a most dangerous idea, and it is a warning, if I may say so, of what might happen were this minority to achieve the control which some people believe, and perhaps for good reason, that they hope to acquire throughout the world. For that reason, if for no other, I and the group to which I belong are utterly opposed to any surrender of the sovereignty of the British empire or of Canada. We are all part of the British empire. We believe in it. Within the British empire all peoples, including minorities, have had better and fairer treatment than under any other that has existed on earth.
I do not feel able to continue to-night, but I hope to make a few more remarks later on in this debate.

Mr. Chairman, I hesitated to say anything earlier in this debate, although the question of external affairs is one in which I am deeply interested. There is a great deal to be said in regard to the matter that was referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and by the hon. member for North Battleford. It is amazing that any hon. member in this house could speak so lightly at this time on that question, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw did in the question he asked. It shows a callousness of mind and an emotional immaturity that is hardly understandable in an hon. member of this house.
As the hour is late I shall emphasize only two points. First, I believe that our future depends on working out a foreign policy along with the other nations of the world.
The Prime Minister this morning stated that the time was approaching when we must begin to shape the outline of the new world that is to follow after the war. It is to be regretted that he did not give us more information in regard to what the government's policies are. I believe the time has

Supply-External Affairs
come when we must begin to formulate policies, and in that regard I would say our approach this time must be different from what it was in the period between the last war and the beginning of the present war.
If we are to have a successful international policy-and when I say "we", I mean Canada in cooperation with the other nations of the world'-we must have a positive policy. The trouble with our policy in the period between the first world war and the second world war was that it was not a positive policy for peace; it was a negative policy to avoid war. I well remember the stock answer that we were given in the house when we asked questions about the government's attitude toward such matters as the Spanish affair, or about the shipment of war material to Japan. We were always told by the Prime Minister that his great concern was to avoid war, not to do anything that would give cause for offence. That was the sort of attitude that led to the present war.
I am firmly convinced that the democratic nations of Europe, Great Britain and France particularly, although they are largely responsible for the war, did not wish war, did not want war. did not consciously prepare for it. They were set on maintaining things as they were, of maintaining their privileges, their place in the world. They allowed the aggressors to prosper in order that the armed forces of Germany would crush a workers' revolution, of which they were afraid. Let me repeat that the essential thing in a new foreign policy to prevent war is that in the first place it will be a positive policy.
I am very happy to-night to find myself in accord with nearly all that was said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I think he made a most excellent speech and said many things that needed to be said. I agree with the statement that we must put our trust in a system of collective security when this war is over. I believe also that we must begin building that collective security system now. I see no hope for security for Canada in any combination outside a collective security system that will give security not only to Canada but to every nation in the world.
I was surprised this morning to hear the hon. member for Vancouver South say that the British commonwealth of nations and the United States should form an alliance, and that they should tell the world that they are forming an alliance. I admit the sincerity of the hon. member's approach to the question; but to my mind nothing could be more dangerous at this time than for two of the powerful partners in the united nations to say that they intend to form a close alliance. If the United States and the British commonwealth of nations, two of the large units in the united nations, will form an alliance, what is to prevent Russia and China from forming an alliance? We would have again the same old power blocks, one against the other.
I may not know a great deal about international affairs, but I submit that that is not the way in which world peace can be maintained. We have before us a choice of one of two things. We have a choice of being a partner in a system of collective security, where each nation in that collective system will have protection against aggression from any quarter, or we can go along forming alliances and building up balances of power, which policy will ultimately lead to a war such as that in which we are now engaged. Any system of security will also have to be one based on the equality of the nations.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said this evening that we of the British empire, or the British commonwealth of nations, whichever you like, were a very fine people, indeed, but that unfortunately the rest of the world did not have the exalted opinion of our virtues that we have ourselves. I was recently talking to a gentleman who holds a high position in this country. Some three years ago he had taken advantage of an opportunity of flying from the United Kingdom to Australia by the usual route-Lisbon, along the Mediterranean, crossing to Egypt and Persia and India, and then along the South Sea islands to Australia. He told me that in all the places visited on that trip he did not meet any native peoples who were friendly to the British empire. He said that where they were not neutral as to which of the warring nations they would have rule them, they were definitely hostile. His statement was that their attitude was largely owing to the superior attitude adopted by the people Britain had sent to those countries as governors.
AVhat is said by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques) may be quite true, namely, that by and large the British government has given government as good as or better than any other country. The fact remains, however, that the British government was ruling larger sections of the world than any other country, and governments are usually unpopular. The government you have not is usually better than the one you have.
The War-Sicily

The British empire has a great deal for which it is responsible, because it has had tremendous opportunities.
The hour is late, and I do not wish to say anything further, except that I want again to emphasize that if we are to reap the fruits of the sacrifices of this war; if we are to get some return in peace and prosperity for the young lives that are being sacrificed in this war, we shall get it only through a system of collective security, in which each nation- Canada included-will become a guarantor for the peace and safety of all nations.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
